items.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000, government data shows
items.description: The number of deaths in Democratic Republic ​of Congo’s Ebola outbreak has surpassed 4,000, ‌government data showed on Friday, as the worst epidemic in the country’s history resists containment efforts. The outbreak, caused ​by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, became ​the largest and deadliest in Congo after surpassing the ⁠2018-2020 epidemic. It is now second only to ​the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which infected ​over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Government figures showed on Friday that ​the death toll had risen to 4,018, ​and confirmed cases had reached 8,300 across seven provinces. Over 2,000 ‌patients ⁠have recovered from the disease. Congo’s government and the UN said last month there were signs that transmission was slowing in some parts of Ituri ​province, where ​the outbreak ⁠began. But it continues to spread fast across eastern Congo, including in ​neighbouring North Kivu . South Ubangi province, located in ​the ⁠northwest of the country, became the seventh province to declare the outbreak last month after a ⁠man ​who had travelled from eastern ​Congo died of the virus.

items.title: If the war drags on
items.description: The war in the Middle East has turned a regional conflict into a global economic shock. Prolonged disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up oil, gas, freight and insurance costs, adding to inflation and squeezing growth. Rich economies can absorb part of the shock. Developing countries such as Pakistan cannot. They face larger import bills, weaker external balances, higher inflation and less room for monetary or fiscal relief. What happens in Hormuz is no longer just a Middle Eastern security crisis. It is an economic threat to countries far beyond the battlefield. Seven months after the first US-Israel strikes on Iran , the Strait of Hormuz still sets the mood of the world economy. Roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies pass through it. Brent traded below $68 a barrel in mid-February. It now sits around $100. The diplomacy has been real, and it has been squandered. Pakistan hosted US and Iranian delegations in April after the two sides agreed to a two-week ceasefire. An interim agreement collapsed shortly after it was announced in June. More recently, Iran tabled a revised plan on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. It asked for frozen funds to be released, oil sanctions lifted and the naval blockade ended in four to five days, with nuclear talks starting within seven. Seven months after the first US-Israel strikes on Iran, the Strait of Hormuz still sets the mood of the world economy Tehran ties any reopening of Hormuz to those steps. President Donald Trump called the plan unacceptable. Washington has since replied through Qatari mediators, and Trump denies offering sanctions relief. Both capitals are gambling with other people’s money. Washington believes the blockade will exhaust Tehran first. Tehran believes a shut strait will exhaust Americans. Each may be partly right. Neither calculation counts the cost to importing economies that had no say in the war. The global numbers look calm only on the surface. The International Monetary Fund’s July update projects world growth of three per cent this year but raised its inflation forecast to 4.7pc. The damage shows up in prices rather than output, and it lands hardest on commodity importers. Developing Asia shows how. The Asian Development Bank’s (ADB) September outlook has regional growth slowing from 5.5pc last year to 5pc in 2026. Inflation is held at 4.2pc only because governments are absorbing higher energy costs through costly subsidies, and someone will pay for those later. Earlier ADB modelling warned that if disruption lasts beyond a year, the region could lose up to 1.3 percentage points of growth over FY27, with South Asia facing the sharpest price pressure. Pakistan sits squarely in that group. Consumer prices rose 10.26pc year on year in September, and the State Bank held its policy rate at 11.5pc, leaving little room to ease. Petroleum makes up about a third of imports, and each $10 per barrel adds an estimated $1.8-2 billion to the annual oil bill. The cushion is the Gulf. Overseas Pakistanis remitted a record $41.6bn in FY26, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE supplied $18.6bn of it. That cushion holds only if the war does not spread. Diplomacy is the cheaper option, and two capitals have invested in it. Islamabad has kept channels open to Washington, Tehran and the Gulf. Pakistan’s push to renew US-Iran talks had Chinese backing. Beijing has its own reasons. It is Iran’s largest trading partner and a big buyer of Gulf crude, and a closed strait hurts it. After their Beijing summit in May, Trump said China’s President Xi Jinping had offered to help end the war and wanted Hormuz reopened. The White House added that Xi opposed any toll for using the strait. At the White House on 24 September, he said he supported a return to the interim agreement. No breakthrough was reported, and China’s readout discussed the Middle East without naming the Iran war. The war has also exposed the limits of American power. Trump wanted it over by the end of March, according to the US media, and on 9 March he claimed the strait had reopened. Seven months on, it has not. The world’s strongest navy has not forced Hormuz open, and the blockade of Iranian ports has not made Tehran concede. Washington asked allies to help secure the waterway, and most were reluctant to enter an active war zone. Before the Beijing summit, Trump said he did not need help on Iran. He then pressed Xi for it, and in September he greeted the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Brookings concluded that Xi held the upper hand. The mediators that matter are Pakistan, Qatar and Oman. Force alone has not delivered what Washington wanted, and other capitals now hold pieces of any settlement. Both sides now need to concede something small to gain something big. Washington should accept sequencing: a verified reopening of Hormuz in exchange for easing the blockade, with nuclear questions in a separate, time-bound round. Tehran should drop transit tolls, which even its largest trading partner opposes, and accept independent verification. Neither side has shown it can win outright. The US has the strongest navy afloat and has not reopened the strait. Iran has absorbed seven months of strikes and has not broken the blockade. Middle Eastern crude exports have climbed to their highest level since the war began, a sign that markets are ready for peace. The mediators in Islamabad and Doha are ready. The principals are the missing piece. Five months remain before the war’s first anniversary and the ADB’s worst case. That is enough time for a deal, if Washington and Tehran sit down and stay there. The writer is a Dawn staffer Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, October 5th, 2026

items.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
items.description: Rebel forces in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said it made the decision to relocate due to concerns about risks to civilians. Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city. Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces, alongside allied fighters, in parts of Ethiopia’s northern regions of Tigray, Afar, and Amhara. The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries. The US Department of State called for “restraint” and “dialogue” on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia’s neighbours about the conflict in Egypt. Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides. However, over the last six months, relations have worsened, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government from power. The civil warwas one of the most deadly conflicts this century – the AU’s mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance – an allegation that it denied. Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period. The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

items.title: All set for 7th Ghana Credit Excellence Awards 2026 on October 10
items.description: All is set for the 7th Ghana Credit Excellence Awards 2026 on 10 th October, 2026, as leaders in the banking and finance industry converge to celebrate outstanding performance, innovation and leadership across the country’s banking, microfinance and credit management landscape. The event that comes off at the Vice Chancellors Complex, Legon, Accra, is expected to bring together executives and professionals from universal banks, community banks, microfinance institutions, debt collection agencies and other players within Ghana’s financial ecosystem to celebrate a year of resilience, growth and transformation. A platform for excellence and national development Since its inception, the Ghana Credit Excellence Awards has grown into one of the notable events on Ghana’s financial services calendar. Organised annually by the Chartered Institute of Credit Management Ghana (CICMG), the awards recognise institutions and individuals whose performance, leadership and professional contributions have helped strengthen ethical standards, financial inclusion and the broader development of Ghana’s financial sector. This year’s edition comes at an important time for the industry. Ghana’s banking sector has in recent years navigated a challenging macroeconomic environment characterised by inflationary pressures, exchange-rate volatility and evolving regulatory requirements. Against this backdrop, improvements in profitability, asset quality and balance-sheet performance across parts of the banking sector have contributed to renewed confidence in the industry. The 2026 awards therefore go beyond celebrating individual achievements. They provide an opportunity for the industry to reflect on its progress, recognise institutions and leaders that have demonstrated resilience, and highlight the standards needed to build a stronger and more inclusive financial system. The awards are not simply about recognition but also about reinforcing the values required to support Ghana’s economic development. “The Ghana Credit Excellence Awards is not just about celebration. It is a platform that reinforces the values of sound credit management, ethical leadership and financial inclusion that are critical to Ghana’s economic development, said Agyapong Amo, Executive Secretary of CICMG Awards categories reflect the breadth of the sector A defining feature of the Ghana Credit Excellence Awards is the breadth of its categories, which recognise institutional performance, brand strength and individual leadership across different segments of Ghana’s financial services industry. Business Excellence Awards The Business Excellence category will recognise top-performing institutions, including: Bank of the Year Community Bank of the Year Microfinance Bank of the Year Credit Union of the Year Debt Collection Agency of the Year Brand Excellence Awards The Brand Excellence category will honour institutions that have demonstrated strong and trusted brand positioning within the loans and advances services marketplace, including: Community Bank Brand of the Year Microfinance Bank Brand of the Year Microcredit Brand of the Year Leadership Awards The Leadership Awards will spotlight individuals whose leadership has contributed significantly to institutional performance and the development of Ghana’s financial sector. Categories include: Managing Director/CEO of the Year – Bank Chief Executive Officer of the Year – Community Bank Chief Executive Officer of the Year – Microfinance Bank Woman of Excellence Leadership in Credit of the Year The evening will also feature a Lifetime Achievement Award, recognising an individual whose sustained contribution to Ghana’s credit and financial sector has created a lasting professional legacy. Together, the categories demonstrate CICMG’s commitment to recognising excellence across the financial sector—not only among large universal banks, but also within community banking, microfinance and credit union institutions that play an important role in expanding access to financial services, particularly in underserved and rural communities. Why the 2026 awards matter The timing of this year’s ceremony is particularly significant as Ghana’s financial sector continues to adjust to changing economic and regulatory conditions. The banking industry has benefited from a gradually more supportive macroeconomic environment, with developments in inflation, exchange-rate stability and fiscal conditions helping to strengthen confidence across the sector. Several banks have also recorded improvements in profitability and returns, while continuing to focus on deposit mobilisation, lending and balance-sheet growth. At the same time, community banks and microfinance institutions continue to serve an important role in providing financial services to small businesses, farmers and low-income households, particularly in areas where access to conventional banking services remains limited. Recognising excellence across both ends of the financial-services spectrum reinforces the broader mission of the Ghana Credit Excellence Awards: to celebrate excellence wherever it occurs across Ghana’s diverse financial landscape. The awards also complement CICMG’s professional mandate of promoting sound credit management, professional development and higher standards among practitioners within the credit, risk and financial-services professions. A night of recognition, leadership and networking Guests attending the 2026 ceremony can expect an evening combining recognition, industry dialogue and networking. The event is expected to feature remarks from distinguished personalities drawn from Ghana’s financial and regulatory establishment, providing perspectives on developments and challenges shaping the country’s credit and banking landscape. Held under the theme “Beyond Stablisation: Building a Resilent, Inclusive and Sustainable Financial Sector,” underscores the need to consolidate the gains of recent reforms by creating a financial system that not only safeguards stability but also drives investment, entrepreneurship, innovation, job creation, and shared prosperity. The ceremony is expected to attract senior executives, board chairpersons, industry professionals, entrepreneurs, and other stakeholders. The red-carpet arrivals from 5:00 p.m. will set the tone for an evening celebrating the achievements of institutions and individuals whose contributions extend beyond financial performance to include ethical leadership, innovation, professionalism and national development. A celebration of excellence As the countdown to Thursday, October 8, 2026, continues, anticipation is building within Ghana’s financial community. For the institutions and individuals recognised at this year’s Ghana Credit Excellence Awards, the occasion will represent more than an accolade. It will serve as recognition of past performance and a benchmark for continued excellence. For CICMG, the awards reaffirm the Institute’s commitment to promoting professional standards, ethical credit management and responsible leadership while celebrating the individuals and institutions helping to shape the future of Ghana’s financial sector.

items.title: Portugal keeps door open for star Ronaldo to return
items.description: REUTERS

items.title: El tirón de Vox mantiene al bloque de la derecha en el 50% en plena conmoción por Maricarmen
items.description: Solo un partido avanza: Vox. El resto retrocede. Y el PP, pese a que es el que más pierde, sigue al frente de un bloque derechista en números de mayoría absoluta en plena conmoción por el caso Maricarmen . Así es el balance de ganadores y perdedores que arroja el último barómetro de voto de 40dB. para EL PAÍS y la Cadena SER , elaborado con 2.000 entrevistas online entre el 25 de septiembre (dos días después del mediático desahucio y con la acampada en Sol ya lanzando sus proclamas) y el 28 (un día antes de que el Ejecutivo aprobara los dos decretos con los que ha intentado — sin éxito — dar una respuesta urgente a la conmoción social suscitada por el caso). Seguir leyendo

items.title: Consulte todos los datos internos de la encuesta de EL PAÍS: cuestionarios, cruces y respuestas individuales
items.description: EL PAÍS y la Cadena SER publican el barómetro mensual de octubre realizado por la empresa 40dB. Ofrecemos acceso libre y gratuito a todas las bases de datos sobre las que se fundamenta el trabajo sociológico. Seguir leyendo Presentación del informe del Barómetro mensual Datos completos Accederá a una carpeta con el informe de resultados, cuestionario, los datos con las respuestas individuales y el análisis de cruces, entre otros documentos. Varios formatos disponibles

items.title: Manual de resistencia de los chalecos naranjas: de la asamblea de bienvenida al “pagamos, pero no nos vamos”
items.description: Han sido cuatro años de activismo. Su lucha no comenzó el 23 de septiembre, cuando Maricarmen Abascal salió en camilla de su casa mientras era desahuciada. Alrededor de 160 activistas llevaban mucho tiempo reuniéndose en asambleas y organizando estrategias de desobediencia para confeccionar una especie de manual de resistencia. “Lo que le pasó a Maricarmen no empezó el miércoles. Empezó muchos años antes”, ha repetido Valeria Racu, portavoz del Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Inquietud en el PSOE y Sumar por el mensaje contra “la política”
items.description: El tiempo de los políticos ha terminado; es el tiempo de la calle. Este lema recorrió todo el fin de semana numerosas ciudades de España, impulsado por el movimiento del Sindicato de Inquilinas. Ese desdén por lo institucional estuvo presente desde el nacimiento de la protesta. “¿Dónde está el Gobierno progresista?”, es la pregunta del movimiento, fuertemente crítico con la acción gubernamental, aunque haya más énfasis en el grito contra la especulación, el rentismo, los fondos buitre y el PP por no facilitar suelo a través de sus ayuntamientos ni planes de vivienda en sus comunidades autónomas. ¿Pero, insisten, dónde ha estado el Gobierno en el impulso de la legislación para limitar precios en el alquiler y detener los desahucios? Se obvia la mayoría parlamentaria, que ha impedido la aprobación de 14 decretos. Y algunas iniciativas de protección a los más vulnerables que empezaron con la pandemia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Maruja Torres: “No tengo el coño para equidistancias en este momento”
items.description: Maruja Torres (Barcelona, 83 años) camina con bastón, pero su cabeza va a la velocidad de la luz y su lengua vuela como un avión supersónico. Es miércoles a mediodía y lleva desde temprano yendo y viniendo. Se ha despertado a las siete, ha devorado la prensa en el desayuno, ha hecho sus ejercicios, se ha vestido, se ha maquillado, ha salido a la calle y ya ha dado una entrevista con motivo de la publicación de su nuevo libro, Cuanta más gente me jode, más buenos momentos tengo (Temas de Hoy). En el vestíbulo del hotel donde ha citado a EL PAÍS, se cruza con Soraya Sáenz de Santamaría [ex vicepresidenta del Gobierno conel PP}, que se acerca a saludarla. En unos días quedará con los Reyes, que la han invitado a un acto en Oviedo. Torres lleva toda la vida moviéndose y de eso trata su libro, de sus viajes por el mundo: París en abril del 68, Beirut en el 87, Hollywood en los noventa... Los buenos reporteros saben que el movimiento es vida. Por eso ella sigue. Pide un Negroni, coge aliento y sigue. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Arde Bogotá ensancha los límites del rock español con su inspirado nuevo disco
items.description: Cuando el rock español joven parecía un asunto marginal y limitado a una escorada minoría, llegó Arde Bogotá y lo llevó de nuevo a la cima, a llenar pabellones, a arrastrar a miles de seguidores a festivales, a conseguir que un público amplio vibre con las guitarras rotundas y las canciones viscerales. A las mieles del éxito suele acompañarlas el recelo de una parte del público y de algunos críticos, sectores ambos ruidosos y llenos de suspicacias. Desde que el cuarteto de Cartagena se transformó en un acontecimiento musical de envergadura, se abrió la veda en busca de vetas que alimenten la desconfianza hacia su propuesta. Esta tendencia va a seguir después del previsible éxito de su tercer disco, de título tan rimbombante, Manufacturas del Club de la Gente Sola. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ceuta | La lucha de los que no quieren volver
items.description: Sabil tiene 16 años y hace más de 60 días cruzó a nado la frontera con Marruecos desde su ciudad, Tetuán. Llegó solo y sin dinero. Ahora vive en las naves del Tarajal y busca una plaza en un centro de acogida donde comenzar de nuevo. Lamia llegó embarazada de ocho meses a Ceuta desde Tánger con su marido y su hijo de 15 años. Su bebé Hussei acaba de nacer y viven en la calle esperando un plaza en un centro de mujeres. Naia llegó desde Castillejos con su hija pequeña buscando en España los derechos que su país le niega por ser una mujer separada. Este reportaje en vídeo es un recorrido por la vida de mujeres y menores migrantes en busca de una oportunidad por una vida mejor al otro lado de la frontera. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Siempre fueron fascistas
items.description: El Silicon Valley de la era Obama parecía demócrata. Gente como Eric Schmidt , Sheryl Sandberg y Marisa Meyers no solo donaban con generosidad sino que organizaban las grandes galas que recaudaban fondos para sus campañas. También sus empleados: en 2012, el 83% de las donaciones de los empleados de las principales empresas tecnológicas fueron para él. En su libro The Nerd Reich, el periodista estadounidense Gil Duran señala la victoria del primer presidente negro y la crisis financiera como el principio del fin de ese romance. Las tecnológicas crecieron mientras el resto del mundo se encogía , en parte gracias al apoyo y la confianza de la administración americana. Al mismo tiempo empezaron a declararla obsoleta e ineficaz. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Bruselas plantea retirar el derecho al voto a los nuevos miembros de la UE si no cumplen las reglas
items.description: La Comisión Europea no quiere que la ampliación para integrar a Ucrania, Moldavia y los Balcanes pierda impulso por la turbulenta situación geopolítica en Europa. Y se propone acelerarla. Para ello, ha diseñado una nueva estrategia que busca cambiar las reglas para hacer más rápido y previsible el camino hacia la UE, y plantea medidas para integrar a los países candidatos antes de que sean miembros de pleno derecho, pero también recortar su derecho al voto los primeros años de membresía, e incluso suspenderlo si no cumplen las reglas y no siguen los estándares comunitarios. Bruselas advierte de la necesidad de reformas para que el club, que hoy funciona con 27 socios, pueda seguir avanzando con más de 30. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La Fiscalía se opone a las tres últimas semilibertades del Gobierno vasco a presos de ETA
items.description: La decisión del Gobierno vasco del último mes de conceder o ampliar la semilibertad a tres presos de ETA se ha encontrado con la oposición frontal de la Fiscalía de la Audiencia Nacional. El ministerio público ha presentado recurso a todas ellas al considerarlas prematuras. El último, al tercer grado o régimen abierto de Idoia Mendizábal, alias Iliargi , según ha confirmado EL PAÍS en varias fuentes jurídicas. Antes que al de ella, la Fiscalía ya se había opuesto en las últimas semanas a las semilibertades de Henri Parot, Unai , y de la exjefa etarra Soledad Iparragirre, Anboto . El juez de Vigilancia Penitenciaria José Luis Castro aún debe pronunciarse sobre todas ellas. En todos los casos, las asociaciones de víctimas habían mostrado su malestar por los acuerdos del Ejecutivo de Vitoria. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Dos años de Perelló al frente del Poder Judicial: sin comparecer en el Congreso y con una brecha entre los dos sectores
items.description: Este mes de septiembre se han cumplido dos años desde que los 20 vocales que conforman el Consejo General del Poder Judicial (CGPJ) se pusieran de acuerdo para nombrar a la primera presidenta que ejerce la más alta representación tanto del órgano de gobierno de los jueces como del Tribunal Supremo. Isabel Perelló afronta un nuevo curso que, según algunas fuentes internas, será complejo para poder sacar los principales nombramientos pendientes de magistrados en la cúpula judicial, debido a las fracturas que, tras las negociaciones de estos años, han surgido entre el bloque conservador y el bloque progresista. Perelló tiene pendiente, además, comparecer en el Congreso de los Diputados como marca la ley, algo que no ha hecho desde que llegó al poder. Según fuentes del Consejo, la no comparecencia obedece al retraso con el que se han entregado las memorias judiciales. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La Audiencia ordena investigar el borrado de emails de la exedil que denunció por acoso sexual al alcalde de Móstoles
items.description: La Audiencia Provincial de Madrid ha ordenado al Juzgado de Instrucción nº 1 de Móstoles que reabra la investigación sobre el borrado de la bandeja y archivos de correo electrónico de la exconcejala del PP que denunció al alcalde de dicha localidad madrileña, el popular Manuel Bautista, por acoso sexual y laboral. El hackeo de su correo electrónico oficial se produjo el 7 de noviembre de 2024, días después de que acudiera a su última reunión con dirigentes del PP madrileño y del Gobierno regional para denunciar la conducta del alcalde. Entre la documentación borrada estaban los mensajes intercambiados con el Gabinete de la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, en los que denunciaba el hostigamiento al que supuestamente la sometía Manuel Bautista por no acceder a sus requerimientos sexuales. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ortega Smith: “Mi patriotismo español me impide la cobardía de irme a casa”
items.description: Javier Ortega Smith-Molina (Madrid, 58 años), exsecretario general y exvicepresidente de Vox, ha pasado a engrosar la larga lista de disidentes del partido que fundó hace 13 años. Ya no es portavoz en el Ayuntamiento de Madrid ni portavoz adjunto en el Congreso, pero sigue siendo concejal no adscrito y diputado del Grupo Mixto y ahora ocupa el despacho que perteneció a José Luis Ábalos antes de que lo llevaran preso, puerta con puerta con el de Ione Belarra, un vecindario tan heterogéneo como la propia España. Pese al desengaño con sus antiguos correligionarios, no parece a punto de tirar la toalla. Más bien al contrario: dispuesto a librar nuevas batallas, solo o en compañía de otros. El pasado lunes recuperó un protagonismo indeseado al difundir EL PAÍS la grabación de una charla con su exjefa de prensa en el Ayuntamiento de la que se deducía que la cesó por no acudir a ningún pleno estando de permiso por maternidad . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Amnistía Internacional proyecta sobre Marruecos la sombra de las escuchas de espionaje
items.description: Los servicios de inteligencia de Marruecos disponen de distintos programas de ciberespionaje, además del más conocido, el israelí Pegasus : controlan las comunicaciones en zonas de tránsito de los aeropuertos y se infiltran en tiendas de telefonía para infectar móviles. Así lo asegura una reciente investigación de Amnistía Internacional (AI), que proyecta nuevas sombras sobre la red de escuchas de espionaje del país magrebí. La ONG con sede en Londres ha contado en sus últimas pesquisas con el testimonio de un exagente de inteligencia marroquí, que denuncia la existencia de un entramado de vigilancia masiva destinado a rastrear y, en última instancia, a silenciar a periodistas, activistas y disidentes mediante el uso de grabaciones obtenidas de su vida pública y privada. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Cómo se calcula mi sueldo? ¿Mi turno depende de algoritmos? La nueva información que puedes exigir desde hoy en tu contrato
items.description: El contrato de trabajo es la base de cualquier relación laboral, donde quedan establecidas las condiciones por las que el empleado acepta dedicar su tiempo y esfuerzo a una empresa a cambio de una retribución. Desde este lunes 5 de octubre , la información que los contratantes deben facilitar a los nuevos contratados (ya sea en el contrato o en un documento anexo) es más extensa que la que debían entregar hasta ahora, datos que también tienen derecho a exigir los ya empleados. El cambio se debe a un nuevo decreto impulsado por el Ministerio de Trabajo y que transpone la directiva sobre condiciones laborales transparentes y previsibles en la Unión Europea. Entra en vigor hoy, pese a que debía haber quedado sellado en la normativa española como tarde en 2022 . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las mejores series de los últimos meses
items.description: El verano no es el mejor momento para estrenar series. Menos aún si encima hay un Mundial de fútbol. Quizás por eso este trimestre no ha sido el mejor y, sin embargo, hay un puñado de series notables, algunas entre las mejores que veremos este año. Esta es la selección, una buena forma de navegar por el inmenso catálogo de las plataformas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La batalla de Brigitte Bardot contra los tacones y su influencia en el ‘street style’ hasta hoy
items.description: La actriz Brigitte Bardot (1934-2025) encarnó la otra Revolución Francesa. La del rostro cuya belleza emanaba insurrección, aquella que situaba la conducta desprejuiciada en el centro de la vida; una sublevación en la que el cuerpo despreciaba que lo cosificaran con y sin ropa. En este levantamiento a lo Bardot, los tacones altos también se evitaban, en pos de caminar con los pies descalzos para escenificar que la libertad, el juego y el disfrute están por encima de la rigidez y del convencionalismo. En este 2026 se cumplen 70 años de Y Dios creó a la mujer (1956) , película con la que la intérprete y cantante francesa alcanzó la fama mundial al ser convertida en un mito erótico interpretando a Juliette Hardy. Una historia que triunfó gracias a la poderosa presencia en pantalla de BB, como se comenzó a llamar a la actriz a partir de su estreno. Escrita y dirigida por Roger Vadim (primer marido de Bardot), se convirtió en un éxito en taquilla, pero a España no llegaría hasta la década de los setenta por prohibición de la censura del régimen de Franco. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Historia de la oreja de ‘Terciopelo azul’, la obra maestra de David Lynch: “La tratábamos como a un personaje más porque lo era”
items.description: Solo los cinéfilos más avezados reconocerán el nombre de Jeff Goodwin (65 años, Carolina del Sur). Como el de tantos otros artesanos de leyenda, el nombre de este maquillador y especialista en efectos especiales ha quedado enterrado bajo el de los actores, directores y productores acostumbrados a copar los titulares. Sin embargo, Goodwin puede jactarse de formar parte de la historia del cine gracias a una de sus creaciones: la oreja que desencadena la trama de Terciopelo azul (1986), la obra maestra de David Lynch. “Después de todas estas décadas haciendo cine, Terciopelo azul sigue siendo, sin ninguna duda, la experiencia más importante de toda mi carrera”, cuenta este veterano, ya retirado, que será uno de los invitados del Festival de Sitges (del 8 al 18 de octubre), una de las mayores citas en el mundo para los aficionados al cine de terror y ciencia ficción, coincidiendo con el 40 aniversario del estreno de la película. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La presidenta de Amama sobre los cribados de cáncer de mama: “Nos duele que la sociedad se crea que se ha arreglado el problema”
items.description: Se cumple un año desde que estallara en Andalucía el escándalo de los cribados de cáncer de mama que provocó la mayor crisis del Gobierno de Juan Manuel Moreno (PP). La Junta se vio obligada a poner en marcha un plan de choque para agilizar los diagnósticos y ofrecer garantías sobre los programas de prevención, que incluía la incorporación de 4.000 profesionales sanitarios. Esta semana, el consejero de Sanidad, Antonio Sanz, ha asegurado que en este tiempo “se ha cumplido el 100%” de los compromisos, porque “casi todos” esos especialistas se han contratado y se “han producido mejoras importantes”. Ángela Claverol, presidenta de Amama, la asociación andaluza de mujeres víctimas de cáncer de mama que sacó a la luz los fallos en la comunicación de las pruebas diagnósticas, y Anabel Cano, una de las víctimas de esa negligencia, se convirtieron en los rostros más visibles del movimiento ciudadano que exigió explicaciones y reparación. Ambas reaccionan con una sonrisa escéptica a las palabras del consejero. “No solo no se ha arreglado nada, sino que han conseguido tapar la realidad de lo que ha pasado”, sostiene Claverol. En la conversación mantenida con EL PAÍS en su sede de Sevilla, pasan de la rabia a la frustración cuando abordan el drama y las consecuencias con las que muchas, como la propia Cano, siguen lidiando y la incomprensión por parte de la Junta. “Algunas están rendidas, pero muchas seguimos luchando, por nuestras familias, por todas las mujeres, las que están, las que no están, que querían vivir, y las que vendrán. Seguiremos luchando para que esto se arregle y por la justicia”, advierte Cano. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Why pastors may not be seen – or heard – preaching on buses for much longer
items.description: Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana’s capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on buses that take travellers across the country. Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana. Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread. On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen – and heard – preaching the gospel. Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver; at other times they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the top of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours. The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours. But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end. Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both. The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers. Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023. “I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses,” he told the BBC in Twi, a local language. Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana’s second-largest city. We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law. Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves. “Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible,” he says. Boateng Bismark James and his group start preaching at the bus station before boarding the vehicles The new rules have divided opinion. Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship. One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace. ”I don’t like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance because of the noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I’m on public transport.” In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board. “Get down, I say get down,” he shouts. But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world , others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church. Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers’ consent. “The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope,” she says. Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption. “We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers,” he says. “The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra,” he adds. For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income. “I have been able to take care of my children’s education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching.” Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana 2012, but the law banning it has now been beefed up Ghana’s constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety. Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison. But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban. Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana’s lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban. The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC’s request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom. He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message. “There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people,” he says. For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

items.title: Situationer: Can Afridi strike a balance between agitation & governance?
items.description: WHILE the PTI focuses on political mobilisation to secure Imran Khan’s release, the province it is charged with governing continues to face acute security pressures. At present, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa remains the bastion of PTI’s political power. With the provincial government in its hands, the party enjoys a degree of security that allows it operational space and maneuverability. In the ongoing political contest, KP provides PTI with a crucial fallback option; a platform from which it can continue to function and regroup. But the province has also borne the brunt of terrorist attacks, mostly blamed on the proscribed Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), who Islamabad accuses of using Afghan soil to stage their assaults. Critics accuse the PTI-led KP govt of putting agitation ahead of administration, calling for governor’s rule if things don’t improve Since the outfit renewed its attacks following the breakdown of a ‘ceasefire deal’ in Nov 2022, security forces have conducted several targeted intelligence-based operations along the north-western border, though the PTI-led provincial administration has opposed such actions at times. Data from the Centre for Research and Security Studies’ (CRSS) Annual Security Report 2025 indicated a nationwide rise in fatalities from 2,555 in 2024 to 3,417 in 2025, a 34 per cent increase. KP alone accounted for 711 of these deaths, an 82pc share of the national rise. “In light of these facts and figures, the question that comes to mind is why the majority of terror incidents take place in KP,” military spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry asked at a recent press conference. “The primary reason for this is the politically conducive environment provided [to terrorists], and the political-terror nexus that is flourishing in the province,” he had claimed at the time. The province’s chief executive, Sohail Afridi, has been the focal point of such claims. The federal government has repeatedly criticised the provincial administration over worsening law and order, and accused it of not coordinating with the Centre. For his part, CM Afridi has publicly criticised military operations against terrorist groups in KP, and indicated the party’s preference to negotiate with Afghanistan. The chief minister claims the deteriorating security environment is the result of a failed foreign policy, pursued over the last 22 years. “If a policy is not delivering results and is continuously failing, there is a need to change it,” he said during a recent visit to Kohat, in the wake of a suicide bombing that claimed the lives of several security personnel. Agitator-in-chief Simultaneously, Afridi has been charged with spearheading the protest movement by none other than Imran Khan himself, and has made multiple trips to Islamabad to meet the incarcerated PTI founder, albeit without much success. He has also taken the lead in coordinating the party’s nationwide “street movement”, efforts that culminated in the present protest, following a series of delays and postponements. Professor Faizullah Jan, a journalism professor at the University of Peshawar, said, “I think Afridi has been selected because he is hard-headed like Murad Saeed, indebted to Imran for everything, and being ‘anti-establishment.’ Because of his young age and a lack of experience (in governance and politics), he is unlikely to be a threat to party leadership, unlike Pervez Khattak, Mehmood Khan, and Gandapur.” Critics argue that his focus on agitation, especially at a time when the province faces escalating security threats and growing political pressure, has intensified questions about the PTI-led government’s ability to govern effectively. Coming to mainstream politics from the Insaf Students Federation (ISF), Afridi maintains a natural connection with the youth and claims to operate on the same wavelength as them. As a former special assistant for communication and works to his predecessor, Ali Amin Gandapur, he had previously demonstrated his abilities as a firebrand speaker, effectively articulating the party’s narrative. His approach to political mobilisation is, therefore, inseparable from the broader PTI strategy, which is central to understanding the province’s current state of unrest. For his administration, the challenge is not merely resisting pressure from the Centre, but demonstrating that governance can proceed even amid political mobilisation. “Despite the KP chief minister’s combative mood, they (provincial government) want a working relationship [with the federal government],” Ahmed Bilal Mehboob of the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development and Transparency (Pildat) told Dawn. “Imposing governor’s rule will cause more agitation,” he added. “Both the KP and federal governments need to coexist.” Precarious balance His detractors would have you believe that this is not possible. Describing the PTI’s rule, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi says the party has been unable to balance political agitation with its administrative responsibilities, and has neglected issues such as terrorism, corruption and problems faced by medical staff and university faculty, among other issues. “They don’t pay attention to these provincial issues; they only care about agitation and the march to Islamabad and what people are saying about them on social media, so they can one-up each other,” the governor says. “There are three or four groups within them (the PTI) which do not agree with each other.” Mr Kundi said that whenever he speaks with the president, prime minister or interior minister, he informs them that the provincial government “is not seriously monitoring the law and order situation”. “They do not attend the funerals of army officers and personnel and these people want to go off to Islamabad. There are a lot of issues,” he says. But how does the PPP leader - whose own party has spearheaded protests against the Centre in recent months - justify his criticism when another party opts for a similar course of action? Giving examples of PPP and Jamaat-i-Islami protests in recent months, Mr Kundi notes that this political agitation was largely peaceful. “We marched from Karachi to Islamabad with Bilawal sahib without incident,” he recalled. “But when the PTI protests, they spread chaos. You can see it even now; the CM is making statements about what he will do when he gets to Islamabad. He wants chaos.” But even Mr Kundi, who has been making a case for imposing governor’s rule in the province for quite some time now, does not believe that this option can be exercised lightly. In his view, governor’s rule is a “constitutional option”, which should only be treated as “a last resort” for when the situation in the province severely deteriorates. “The president and prime minister sit down with institutions and assess the situation. If they find that it is necessary to use governor’s rule to resolve the situation in the province, they can impose it,” he explained, recalling that the option had been used in the past as well. Militancy in the mix So, what is really at stake here? According to Riccardo Valle, a research analyst tracking militancy across South and Central Asia and co-founder of The Khorasan Diary , local grievances, the absence of the state and poor governance were detrimental to the broader security environment where counter-terrorism policy is enacted, limiting its effectiveness. On the other hand, he noted that constant pressure from militants against security forces poses a major hindrance to any comprehensive effort by the government to address social and economic issues, as security issues prevent the solving of the matter. When asked what policies the KP government could implement to counter terrorists, Mr Valle noted that it “cannot become the sole issue or responsibility of a single province”. Friction between the provincial administration and the Centre could “ultimately benefit militant groups, who can exploit confusion and disagreement both from a narrative-building perspective as well as by increasing pressure on security forces,” he said. Asked about why the KP government is so opposed to military operations, he noted that operations brought mixed results, citing the 2009 Operation Rah-i-Nijat and 2014’s Operation Zarb-i-Azb. “While these operations displaced militants and led to effective control of territories, they also caused collateral damage, internal displacement and profound social [and] economic issues,” Valle explained. “Today, the asymmetric warfare adopted by militant organisations in KP further complicates the efficacy of any such military operation, possibly exacerbating the conflict and alienating local communities,” he added. Nadir Guramani in Islamabad, and Ismail Khan and Manzoor Ali in Peshawar also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, October 5th, 2026

items.title: Oil slips as Middle East crude exports rise, G7 to release stocks
items.description: Oil prices edged lower on Monday as rising ​Middle East crude exports and a release of oil stocks by the Group of Seven ‌nations boosted supplies, offsetting concerns about further damage to Gulf oil infrastructure amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. Brent crude futures fell 66 cents, or 0.65%, to $101.59 a barrel at 0240 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $90.12 a barrel, down 95 ​cents, or 1.03%. Brent gave up most of its gains last week while WTI was 1.6% lower ​after G7 countries agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from ⁠emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from energy export restrictions after pressure from US President Donald Trump. The ​release will add to Middle Eastern crude exports which rose above pre-war levels in four of the seven days of ​the final week of September, shipping data showed on Monday, despite attacks on vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz. “The G7 decision to tap strategic reserves is taking some of the immediate supply anxiety out of the price, while there’s a growing view ​that Saudi export volumes are moving back toward pre-war levels, even if those barrels are still moving at ​higher cost and via less efficient routes,” said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade. “That combination is enough to subdue prices ‌for now ⁠even though the risks of further damage to energy infrastructure around the Gulf region haven’t gone away.” The Houthis said they launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in response to 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours. There was no ​confirmation from Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, ​Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised ⁠government said it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis. Meanwhile, Aramco has unexpectedly cut November crude oil prices ​for Asia to six-year lows. Brent prices continue to stay above $100 per barrel on ​persistent geopolitical tensions ⁠and an increase in attacks on commercial vessels in the Gulf, ING analysts said in a note. Meanwhile, OPEC+ delayed a review that would determine 2027 oil output quotas for its members after the Iran war disrupted projects to expand capacity ⁠across the ​Middle East, throwing estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, said ​two sources close to the matter. In Europe, Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy told Reuters in an ​interview published on Saturday.

items.title: France to step up Ebola funding in Congo amid resurgence fears, minister says
items.description: France will step up its support for efforts to eradicate Ebola in eastern Democratic Republic of ​Congo, Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Saturday during ‌a visit to a region hit by the virus, warning that it could quickly resurge if vigilance waned. * Barrot made rare ​trip by a Western leader to the northeastern Congolese ​city of Bunia , where a laboratory-confirmed case of mpox ⁠was identified in mid-September. * France allocated €13.4 million ($15.1 million) to ​the fight against Ebola between January and July. * Barrot said ​he would propose additional humanitarian funding for Ebola during upcoming French budget discussions. * France’s response came through humanitarian aid, medical research and ​the PRISM programme launched during President Emmanuel Macron’s 2023 ​visit. * A national humanitarian conference is to be held in Paris on ‌October ⁠6, during which Ebola is to be discussed. * “Ebola may seem far away to some people or political leaders, but it can return very quickly. Our responsibility is to prevent ​those resurgences,” ​Barrot told reporters ⁠in Bunia. * Barrot praised Congolese authorities, UN agencies, humanitarian organisations and medical workers for ​containing the epidemic and preventing it from ​spreading to ⁠major urban centres in Congo and beyond. * “There is no need to fear or worry. First and foremost, we must fight ⁠the ​epidemic where it emerges,” Barrot said ​when asked whether it could spread after a case was reported in ​France.

items.title: Only ‘just, fair’ talks can end war, Iran tells US
items.description: TEHRAN: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi declared on Sunday that there was no military solution to the US’ war against the Islamic Republic and that only negotiations based on “justice and fairness” could end the conflict, as talks between Washington and Tehran appeared to be at an impasse. “If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Araghchi told a gathering of foreign ambassadors in Tehran. “There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he continued, adding “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict. Tensions continue to centre on the standoff between the US and Iran regarding the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical conduit for Gulf oil and gas. Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf reiterated that the vital Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met. “The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, are met,” he was quoted by state media as saying. Ghalibaf added that Washington “must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over”. Iranian and US officials held indirect talks last week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, during which Tehran said it presented its seven conditions. The conditions include a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade. US President Donald Trump publicly rejected the proposal while leaving the door open to both further talks and renewed military operations. The US nonetheless replied to Tehran’s proposal last week, with Qatar shuttling messages between the two sides in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the strait. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said that the latest US counterproposals were “more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue”, but that Tehran’s focus was on Hormuz. “We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required an end to disruption of Iranian maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions. He denied that Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its facilities in exchange for sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions. The US has not struck Iran since Sept 1 but has continued a fresh military buildup. Axios reported that Washington had deployed additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to protect energy facilities, and that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group was heading to the Middle East. Iran’s army, meanwhile, said it would upgrade the range of its missiles, underlining Tehran’s warning that it is preparing for further confrontation even as it continues to call for diplomacy. Separately, Iran’s Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned and Hamid Bovard, chief executive of the government-owned National Iranian Oil Company, will be in charge of the ministry as acting minister, state media said on Sunday, without providing a reason for the resignation. Mohsen Paknejad has been the oil mini­ster of the Opec member country since August 2024 and resigns as the seven-month war between Iran and the US puts pressure on the country’s economy. “With acceptance of Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation by Dr Pezeshkian [the country’s president], Hamid Bovard has been appointed as acting oil minister”, state media cited an official at the president’s office as saying. Paknejad was cited by state media, ahead of the news of his resignation, as saying “revenues of the oil that we have sold are still coming and that will continue God willing”. Published in Dawn, October 5th, 2026

items.title: Djokovic beats Zverev to reach China Open semis
items.description: Novak Djokovic battled back from a set down to defeat top seed Alexander Zverev and book his place in the China Open semi-finals. The 39-year-old Serbian triumphed 4-6 6-4 6-4 against world number two Zverev and will play Daniil Medvedev in the last four. Djokovic’s victory over Zverev dented the German’s quest to finish the year as the world’s number one-ranked player. “These are the kind of moments that I still play for, compete for,” Djokovic said. “The motivation is big when you are feeling good and competing at par with the best players in the world in front of 15,000 people. “These are the kind of moments that define dreams, I think, of every tennis player.” In their first meeting in just under 16 months, Djokovic initially struggled to handle Zverev’s power, and the 29-year-old secured the first set after capitalising on a break in the first game. However, Djokovic managed to work his way back into the contest, and the 24-time Grand Slam winner seized an opportunity with a break at 5-4 in the second set to level the match. Little separated the pair in the third set, but the veteran struck again at 5-4 on Zverev’s serve to clinically seal victory. It took Djokovic’s unbeaten tally in Beijing to 32 matches as he moved a step closer to a seventh China Open title and a first trophy of what has been a difficult 2026, with form and fitness proving challenging. “It’s been a struggle this year for different reasons,” Djokovic added. “But I’m still there, still grinding, still making the youngsters work for their money. I’m just glad to push it through.” Djokovic will face third seed Medvedev, who earlier overcame Francisco Cerundolo 7-6 (7-4) 6-3, on Monday. Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz also progressed to the semi-finals with a 7-6 (7-2) 6-2 win over Karen Khachanov. He will play Australia’s Alex de Minaur who was off the pace in the first set against Andrey Rublev before he stepped up to record a 1-6 6-2 6-3 victory.

items.title: US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base amid security concerns
items.description: The United States has moved all of its bombers stationed at RAF Fairford in the United Kingdom back to their home stations in the US, a Pentagon spokesperson said Sunday, following a security incident near the base that is being investigated by British counter-terrorism police. The Pentagon spokesperson said in an email that "all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States," adding that operational security had prevented the US from confirming the movement of its assets and forces in real time. About a dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at RAF Fairford, northwest of London. The aircraft had been used in US military operations against Iran. The US military has also stressed that its bomber force remains capable of conducting operations from the continental United States. The redeployment comes about a week after British police arrested several people in connection with a security incident near the base on September 27. Counter Terrorism Policing said five men in their 20s were initially arrested after three vehicles were reported traveling toward the airbase. The men were arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act, but were later released on police bail and remain under investigation. Police said no improvised explosive devices were found in the vehicles, although a quantity of petrol was recovered. A 27-year-old dual British-Iranian national was subsequently arrested in London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. British counter-terrorism police said on October 3 that he had also been released on bail and that the investigation was continuing. British authorities have raised the possibility of Iranian involvement in the incident. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part, while stressing that the investigation remained complex and ongoing. US President Donald Trump said those behind the suspected plot had planned to cause "big damage," while Secretary of State Marco Rubio referred to the possible involvement of a foreign actor. Iran has rejected the allegations. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on social media that Tehran believed the accusations were misplaced, after Burnham publicly linked Iran to the incident. Iran also summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the allegations. British counter-terrorism officials have not publicly established Iranian responsibility for the incident. On October 1, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said investigators were considering "all possible angles," including possible foreign-state involvement. RAF Fairford has long been used by the US Air Force as a forward operating location for strategic bombers. During the recent conflict with Iran, the base was used to support US military operations, including strikes on Iranian missile sites, according to Reuters. The latest redeployment comes as the investigation into the security incident continues.

items.title: OpenAI safety employee quits, says 'time for trial and error is over'
items.description: A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the company's approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures. Writing in "I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken," published by the Atlantic on Saturday, David Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being "nearly careful enough" and should place greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems. "The time for trial and error is over," Robinson wrote, arguing that advanced AI systems require safeguards more akin to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation. Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what it calls "iterative deployment," releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge. The comments add to a debate within the AI industry over whether companies are moving too quickly to develop increasingly powerful systems. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have faced scrutiny after incidents in which safety controls failed or experimental systems behaved unexpectedly. Robinson, who said he spent three and a half years at OpenAI, helped draft the company's preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches. He wrote: "As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed." "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement. Robinson also warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers' understanding of alignment, a field focused on ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human goals and values.

items.title: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round
items.description: The right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil’s presidential election, beating the incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. But he did not obtain more than 50% of the votes required to win outright. There will be a run-off vote between these two candidates on 25 October. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of the former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup attempt after losing the last election. The election was close, with President Lula polling slightly ahead during the campaign. With 99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro had 47.03% to Lula’s 45.16%. Bolsonaro’s result exceeded expectations, meaning the second round now looks like his to lose, given that some of the other presidential candidates who were knocked out in the first round were right-wing alternatives. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) also had the most governors, senators, and federal deputies elected so far, meaning the party is expected to have the most influence in Congress. The majority of Latin America has now elected right-wing presidents, aligned to the Trump administration, and the run-off will determine whether Brazil – Latin America’s largest country and economy – will follow suit or not. After casting his ballot, Lula, 80, warned that the choice was between democracy and “barbarism”. Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to “free the Brazilian people”. The candidates Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva votes in the general election in Sao Bernardo do Campo Lula and Bolsonaro are the two biggest names in Brazilian politics, on the left and right, and this campaign has polarised Brazil yet again: with themes of sovereignty, crime, the economy and corruption being top concerns for voters. Lula is more popular in Brazil’s poorer northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women. He is seeking a fourth term in office, after being elected in 2002, 2006 and then a later non-consecutive term in 2022. In that election, he beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% of the vote, the closest presidential election result in Brazil’s history. After that election, Bolsonaro’s supporters vandalised government buildings on 8 January 2023. Jair Bolsonaro was banned from running for re-election even before his prison sentence, but endorsed his eldest son Flávio to run in his place. Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle, was elected to the Senate on Sunday. Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to grant his father, and his supporters responsible for the January 8th riots, amnesty if elected. He is more popular in the south, and among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians. Bolsonaro said on Sunday he was “very happy” to have led Lula in the first-round vote, and expressed confidence that he would clinch a run-off victory in three weeks’ time. “I am very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government,” he said, according to AFP. Lula admitted the outcome of the vote was “unexpected”, but insisted that the race was not over. “I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round,” he said on Sunday. “The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people.” US-Brazil relationship The president of Brazil’s supreme electoral court said on Sunday that no evidence of international interference was found in the election. During the campaign, President Lula made “sovereignty” a key pillar of his campaign and at times accused the United States of trying to interfere in and influence Brazil’s elections. He has pledged to increase defence spending. Earlier this year, Flávio Bolsonaro successfully lobbied the United States to designate the two biggest Brazilian gangs as terrorist organisations. In July, Brazil refused visas for two US State Department officials who Brazil alleged were attempting to sow doubt in Brazil’s electoral system, which the US called “baseless.” It came after Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly told a group of foreign diplomats that Brazil’s voting machines share the same origin as Venezuela’s, which is false. Last year, Donald Trump used the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro as justification for imposing tariffs on Brazil and sanctioning some top officials and judges. A win for Flávio Bolsonaro would likely see Brazil join the US’s “Shield of Americas” coalition against narco-trafficking and align more closely with the US. Bolsonaro has pledged though to maintain an “economically pragmatic” relationship with China, which has overtaken the US as Brazil’s biggest trading partner and is a crucial customer for Brazil’s soy and beef exports. Key campaign issues A woman votes at a polling station during Brazil’s general election in Barra de Guaratiba, Rio de Janeiro Corruption became a key issue in this campaign after a scandal involving a jailed banker, Daniel Vorcaro, who orchestrated one of Brazil’s largest financial frauds, embroiled senior figures across the political spectrum. Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged that he’d asked Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m). Lula was also impacted by the scandal indirectly, after police suggested Vorcaro had reached out to the Supreme Court judge Alexandre de Moraes to ask for help avoiding arrest. Moraes denies any wrongdoing. Moraes was not appointed by Lula but is seen as his ally, given Moraes presided over Jair Bolsonaro’s coup trial. Crime and insecurity were also top concerns for voters. Brazil’s homicide rate has fallen, but street crime such as phone thefts, that are highly visible to voters, have increased – and violence and drug trafficking are still major problems. Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to designate Brazilian gangs as terrorists and build maximum-security prisons akin to those in El Salvador. His father, during his presidency, loosened gun ownership restrictions. Flavio Bolsonaro, son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, is leading incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in partial results Lula has criticised the US terrorist designation of Brazilian gangs but has launched various reforms to tackle the financial networks of organised crime networks, improve homicide investigations, and invest in prisons. The economy has been central to this campaign, too: the country has high levels of personal debt and slowing growth. Lula has defined his legacy through a series of social welfare programmes, mostly notably Bolsa Família, that pays families to ensure children stay in education and receive healthcare such as vaccines, as well as building more universities. The programmes have been credited with lifting millions of Brazilians out of poverty. He has backed more investment in data centres and rare earth minerals, which Brazil is rich in, with strong state involvement to ensure that Brazil benefits. He has also backed oil drilling exploration near the mouth of the Amazon River, which has proved controversial with environmentalists, but he has a record of tightening environmental protections and reducing the rate of deforestation in the Amazon. Deforestation increased significantly under Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency. Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged a public debt ceiling and government spending cuts, a revision of social welfare, and to bolster the critical minerals sector.
