items.title: Impact of high US interest rates
items.description: Pakistan faces a less forgiving global financial environment just as its sovereign risk has declined and foreign-exchange reserves have recovered. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury rose above five per cent in late September, touching 5.29pc on September 29, its highest level since 2007. The obvious consequence is that Pakistan will pay more for dollar borrowing. But the effects go further. Persistently high US rates raise the returns demanded on foreign investment, reduce valuations of assets the government wants to privatise, increase the cost of maintaining borrowed reserves and complicate monetary policy at home. Pakistan’s reserves had recovered to $21.4 billion by September 18, an important achievement after the near-crisis of 2023. But reserves represent only one side of a country’s balance sheet. To the extent that they are accumulated through new external liabilities, the headline number can overstate the improvement in the underlying external position. If Pakistan borrows internationally at high rates and some of the proceeds sit in reserves invested in safer, lower-yielding assets, it has purchased valuable insurance against a foreign-exchange crisis — but at a cost. Reserves accumulated through exports do not create the same liability. Over time, what matters is not simply the level of reserves but the economy’s ability to replenish them through its own foreign-exchange earnings. High rates raise the returns demanded on foreign investment, reduce valuations of assets the government wants to privatise, increase the cost of maintaining borrowed reserves and complicate monetary policy High US rates also alter the economics of foreign investment. Pakistan is placing considerable hopes on attracting capital into mining, energy and infrastructure. International investors, however, do not evaluate Pakistani projects in isolation. When US government bonds yielded close to zero, a project offering an expected dollar return of 10pc could appear attractive despite substantial risk. If investors can obtain more than 5pc from US government debt, Pakistani projects must offer appreciably more to compensate for currency, regulatory, political and execution risks. That raises Pakistan’s cost of equity as well as its cost of debt. It also affects privatisation. An asset’s value reflects the present value of its expected future cash flows. Higher discount rates reduce that value. Islamabad may therefore find itself trying to sell assets when expensive global capital is reducing what international investors are prepared to pay. High US rates also complicate monetary policy. The State Bank’s policy rate remains well above US rates, and its primary mandate is domestic price stability. But global rates influence the attractiveness of dollar and rupee assets, external financing conditions and exchange-rate pressures. Pakistan’s capital account is not fully open, so the relationship is not mechanical. Nevertheless, persistently high US yields could narrow the room for domestic easing if inflation or pressure on the rupee were to re-emerge. The more important question concerns the use of foreign capital. A country borrowing dollars at high rates cannot sustainably use those funds for consumption, recurrent expenditure or investments generating inadequate returns. Projects financed by external debt eventually need to produce sufficient economic value — and foreign-exchange earnings or savings — to service that debt. This exposes a longstanding weakness in Pakistan’s development model. The country has often borrowed abroad to finance investments that generate economic activity domestically but limited foreign currency. Roads, power plants and urban infrastructure may raise welfare and productivity, but dollar debt incurred to finance them must ultimately be serviced through exports, remittances, foreign investment or further borrowing. A project can therefore generate an acceptable domestic return while weakening the external balance sheet if the foreign exchange it earns or saves is insufficient to service the external debt incurred to finance it. The problem was easier to obscure when global money was cheap. It becomes harder when the risk-free dollar rate exceeds 5 per cent. Pakistan’s successful $3bn international bond issue in September demonstrates how far market confidence has recovered. It raised $1.75bn through 5.5-year bonds at 7.5 per cent and $1.25bn through 10-year bonds at 7.9 per cent. Renewed market access is valuable, but it also creates a familiar temptation: to interpret the ability to borrow again as evidence that the external problem has been solved. Pakistan has experienced versions of this cycle before. Reserves recover, sovereign spreads decline, and imports rise as economic activity strengthens. Exports fail to accelerate sufficiently and eventually the foreign-exchange constraint returns. Policymakers then seek another International Monetary Fund programme, bilateral rollover or infusion of foreign capital. Higher global rates make repeating that cycle more expensive. Pakistan’s recovery should therefore be judged by more than reserves, the exchange rate or access to international debt markets. The more meaningful test is whether the country’s capacity to generate foreign exchange is improving faster than its external obligations. Borrowing abroad for an investment that expands export capacity or efficiently substitutes for imports is fundamentally different from borrowing dollars for an asset whose revenues will be almost entirely in rupees. Every new foreign loan should face a basic question: where will the dollars to repay it come from? Pakistan cannot control the global price of money. It can reduce its vulnerability to it. The ultimate test of its recovery is not how readily it can borrow dollars when international markets reopen, but whether it can earn enough dollars not to depend on them. The writer is the former head of Citigroup’s emerging markets investments and author of ‘The Gathering Storm’. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, October 5th, 2026

items.title: Train engine derails near Balochistan's Kuchlak
items.description: QUETTA: The engine of the newly launched Jinnah Peoples Train, operating between Kuchlak and Sariab, derailed near Kuchlak Railway Station on Sunday while leaving for its next destination towards Quetta. No casualties were reported and all passengers remained safe. Railway authorities immediately arranged a replacement engine and the train departed for Sariab after a brief delay. According to railway offi­­cials, engine No. 5120 der­a­iled on Line No. 3 on Sunday while reversing dur­ing routine shunting operations. Officials initially attributed the incident to the alleged theft of a fishplate, saying an investigation was under way to determine the actual cause. However, Kuchlak police disputed the railway authorities’ claim and said the derailment was caused by the poor condition of the track, where railway workers had been carrying out work. Railway authorities have ordered an inquiry into the derailment. Published in Dawn, October 5th, 2026

items.title: Modric ‘ashamed’ of Croatia’s ‘catastrophic night’
items.description: Croatia captain Luka Modric said he felt “ashamed” of his side’s performance in Saturday’s 7-0 defeat at home to England in the Nations League. It was the first time in 20 years as an international that the AC Milan midfielder said he had felt such emotion, describing it as a “catastrophic night”. Modric, 41, was making his 205th appearance for his country after recently agreeing to extend his international career under returning manager Slaven Bilic. “You can’t play football like that… we looked like we had four or five players less,” said the former Real Madrid player, who helped Croatia to second-place and third-place finishes at the 2018 and 2022 World Cups during a storied career. “It is difficult to find an explanation for such a performance without duels, fouls, aggressiveness, togetherness. “I’ve been here for 20 years, but for the first time I feel ashamed after a game.” Croatia kicked off Bilic’s second spell in charge with a 2-1 Nations League win away to the Czech Republic that put them above England in Group A3. They followed that up with a chastening 4-1 defeat away to world champions Spain but were still level on points with Thomas Tuchel’s Three Lions before Saturday’s humiliating loss in Rijeka. With the top two qualifying for the latter stages, Croatia had the chance to put themselves in pole position to beat England to a place in the quarter-finals. Yet by the time Modric was substituted in the 57th minute, the home side were already 5-0 down after conceding two goals from Harry Kane and one apiece from Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka. Modric was forced to watch from the sidelines as further goals from Saka and Morgan Rogers extended England’s advantage before the final whistle. Luka Modric watches on as Jude Bellingham congratulates Bukayo Saka for scoring England’s fourth goal in a 7-0 win over Croatia “You can lose, or play against an opponent who is better – and they are right now,” added the former Spurs favourite, who helped Croatia knock England out in the qualifying stages for the 2008 Euros where they reached the quarter-finals in Bilic’s first spell as manager. “But in any case, losing like this and squandering the reputation we’ve built over the years is unacceptable… [it was a] catastrophic night [for Croatia].” It does not get any easier for Croatia, who next host Spain in Split on Tuesday, and will finish their Nations League campaign with games away to England (12 November) and at home to the Czech Republic (15 November). “We need to pull ourselves together, stay together because a new difficult game awaits us,” said Modric, with Croatia third in the table, facing a battle to retain their status in the top tier of the Nations League. “We have to show our true colours, that there is defiance and pride in us, desire, willingness, togetherness, these things cannot be lost overnight.”

items.title: Naqvi, Kundi mull governor’s rule
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Interior Mini­ster Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday called on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi to discuss the political and security situation amid speculations of ‘imminent’ governor’s rule in the province. According to a statement issued by Governor House, both leaders expressed concerns over the “risk of facilitating terrorists to safely cross security checkposts” during the PTI’s Islamabad march. They agreed that whenever the president and the prime minister deemed it necessary to impose the governor’s rule or emergency to “save the province from terrorism and destruction, the Governor’s House will play a full constitutional role”. They also discussed important matters at the provincial level, including growing unrest in the province, the political scenario, and the situation arising from the Islamabad march. The statement read that the KP government’s attitude during the negotiations regarding counterterrorism actions was tantamount to ‘enmity’ toward the people and the province. Mr Naqvi and Mr Kundi also termed the use of helicopters and other government resources by Afridi and the provincial ministers for the march as a “blatant violation” of the IHC verdict. Mr Kundi said in his own statement that KP Inspector General of Police Zulfikar Hameed was also present at the meeting, which revolved around the prevailing security situation in the province. “The security of our people rem­ains our foremost priority. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has sacrificed enough, and every institution must work together to protect our people and defeat terrorism,” the governor said. A government source told Dawn that the government was seriously considering the imposition of the governor’s rule in KP. “The government believes that its demands regarding KP’s cooperation to curb terrorism were genuine and rightful; thus, there was no logic behind the PTI’s decision to leave the dialogue… the imposition of emergency is imminent,” the source claimed. Published in Dawn, October 5th, 2026

items.title: Klopp’s mixed start continues as Germany held
items.description: Germany’s mixed start under new head coach Jurgen Klopp continued with a goalless Nations League draw against Greece in Thessaloniki. Klopp made three changes as his side looked to avenge a 1-0 loss to Greece in Augsburg last week. But Germany’s dominance did not pay off on a night when they had more than 70% of possession and took 21 shots. Greece had the first chance as Jonas Urbig was forced into a decent save from Fotis Ioannidis’ header in the second minute, but it was largely one-way traffic from there. Jonathan Burkhardt thought he had put the visitors in front in the first half, but a review by the video assistant referee spotted a handball by Tom Bischof in the build-up. Lennart Karl and Derry Scherhant had chances, as did Konstantinos Mavropanos and Giorgos Masouras for the hosts, but neither side proved clinical in front of goal. “We built up quite a bit of pressure but didn’t get that goal,” Germany captain Florian Wirtz said after the game. “That’s frustrating. “Overall, we can be satisfied with how we played. There were a lot of positives. We must not forget that we have only been together for a week. We really wanted the win, but not everything is bad now.” The stalemate signals a frustrating end to the international break for Klopp, who begins his reign with one win from his first four games. Greece remain unbeaten and are second in Group A2, level on eight points with leaders the Netherlands, while Germany are three points behind in third.

items.title: The job interview question you don’t have to answer
items.description: Prepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable. While employers in the UK are within their rights to ask how much you are paid in your current role, applicants are not obliged to disclose it. Recruiters have been encouraged to stop asking about salary history, and in the EU, new rules will prevent them from doing so. But in the UK, there is still a chance it will come up, so how best should you answer? What can interviewers ask? When interviewing or deciding on new staff, employers must not discriminate against an applicant on the basis of so-called protected characteristics, including age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. Sometimes it feels like interviewers and interviewees tip-toe around the subject of money. But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations. She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly. A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag – #EndSalaryHistory. The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality. Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual’s perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation supported the move, urging recruiters not to ask. Employers in the EU will be banned from asking about salary history in new rules being rolled out across the bloc. But that’s not featured in the Cabinet Office’s plans in the UK, which instead focus on telling employers to publish salary information in job adverts . What’s the best way to answer? When you’re applying for a new job, you can disclose your current salary if you’re comfortable. Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary, so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward. There is no requirement to disclose your salary if you don’t want to. Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role. Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid rather than their salary history. Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with “realism but also confidence”. “Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role,” she says. “Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package.”

items.title: Initial indications suggest Flydubai co-pilot acted alone in attack
items.description: Initial findings indicate that the Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking the captain and attempting to take control of an Israel-bound flight appears to have acted alone, rather than as part of an organized group or at the direction of a foreign government, according to multiple US officials familiar with the investigation and a former Israeli security official cited by NBC News. US officials stressed that the investigation into last Wednesday's incident is still in its early stages. Shalom Ben Hanan, a former official with Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet, said the current assessment points to a lone-wolf attack allegedly inspired by material found online. He cautioned, however, that investigators still need to determine whether any organization or state was involved. Emirati authorities, who are overseeing the investigation, said on Saturday that the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain with a crash ax and tried to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls in what they described as an attempted terrorist attack. The suspect, Omani national Hamam Hamami, told Emirati investigators during questioning that he had planned to deliberately crash the passenger jet into Ben Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv, said an Israeli source. According to the source, Hamami told investigators that he had begun planning the attack before being hired by Flydubai. He allegedly researched airlines operating flights to Tel Aviv and sought employment with them before eventually joining Flydubai. The flight was carrying 174 passengers, most of them Israelis, from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The attempted crash was thwarted after crew members and passengers entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker, according to eyewitnesses and Israeli officials. Following the incident, Israel's Transportation Ministry notified foreign airlines that crew members holding sole or dual nationality from any of 27 countries, including Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, are prohibited from operating or traveling as crew on flights to Israel.

items.title: Trump unveils ‘Super Intelligence Force’ to oversee AI policy
items.description: US President Donald Trump says he has created a new task force focused on artificial intelligence (AI), which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. The “Super Intelligence Force” will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology’s development and will coordinate the government’s engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday. Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defence for Research and Engineering Emil Michael will also be part of the task force. Trump said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a “morally binding” pact to regulate the technology. “The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government’s engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organisations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies,” Trump wrote. He also named Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor as a member of the task force, which will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The announcement follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology. In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public. “The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency,” Altman told Politico’s technology-focused newsletter Decoded. Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves. The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google. US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton On the same day, the president also signed an executive order to rename AI as “super intelligence”, after previously saying the word artificial made the technology sound “fake”. Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding , arguing that the use of “super intelligence” could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems. Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm’s AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI. “SpaceX is a super intelligence company”, Musk wrote. The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to join a project studying the future of war. Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump .

items.title: Zirkzee gives Netherlands win as van Dijk joins 100 club
items.description: Joshua Zirkzee scored the winning goal as the Netherlands beat Serbia to move to the top of their Nations League group. The Manchester United forward came on at half-time and restored the hosts’ lead in Eindhoven with a tap-in from Tijjani Reijnders’ pass across goal. Teun Koopmeiners was one of four Dutch changes, making his first start under Xavi, and the Juventus midfielder opened the scoring just after the half-hour mark, finding the far bottom corner with a free-kick whipped in from the right from a crowded box. Four minutes later, Mihajlo Cvetkovic rose above Koopmeiners to head past Bart Verbruggen for his first international goal, drawing Serbia level, but Zirkzee would have the decisive say. It was a special night for Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk, as the 35-year-old centre-back made his 100th international appearance. Van Dijk’s defence mostly thwarted a Serbian side that started strongly but remained winless at the bottom of group A2. Joey Veerman and Reijnders both went close to adding to the Netherlands’ tally, but they did not need a third goal. Winning by the same scoreline against Serbia twice in quick succession – having prevailed in Belgrade seven days prior to this latest meeting – puts them in a strong position with two games remaining. New Netherlands head coach Xavi remains unbeaten after four games in charge, with two wins and two draws.

items.description: Children in North Darfur have been recruited by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), subjected to sexual violence and left facing the effects of starvation and years without education, according to Amnesty International researcher Janine Morna. Children in Sudan are not only being caught up in the violence of war but are also being deliberately targeted, according to researcher Janine Morna of international human rights advocacy organisation Amnesty International. Janine Morna is an Amnesty International human-rights researcher specialising in children affected by armed conflict. Her current role is Thematics Researcher – Children, within Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme. She has researched conflicts in Niger, north-east Syria, Ukraine, Haiti, and Sudan. In an exclusive interview at Radio Dabanga studios in Amsterdam (scroll down for full transcript), Morna describes to Radio Dabanga’s English Editor, Andrew Bergman how the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have recruited boys in North Darfur to fight, herd livestock used by the force, and gather intelligence about opposing forces. Watch the complete interview here She says the investigation found that recruitment happened in different ways. Groups allied with the RSF sometimes worked with community leaders and others to mobilise young people, including older boys and, in some cases, younger children, to fight alongside the force. In other cases, young men and older boys were abducted during attacks on villages and forced or compelled to fight. ‘Children are caught up in the killing, bombardment and displacement, and suffer the same violations as adults, but they are also deliberately targeted for a range of other violations…’ Morna says one RSF leader whose unit numbered about 90 told researchers that around 40 per cent of its members were young people. Girls have faced a different pattern of abuse, she says, with rape and other forms of sexual violence documented in the investigation. When young women were rounded up, there was not necessarily any consideration of whether they were under 18. The youngest case describes by Morna involved a 13-year-old girl who was abducted and gang-raped repeatedly over several days. “Children are caught up in the killing, bombardment and displacement, and suffer the same violations as adults,” she says. “But they are also deliberately targeted for a range of other violations.” Starvation and the impact on young children The investigation, which included interviews with 39 children, also examined the effects of the siege of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, where children struggled to find enough food. Morna says children and babies were particularly vulnerable because they could not survive prolonged food shortages in the same way as adults. Researchers documented cases in which children were not eating regularly and found that four children had died because food was unavailable. She says the actual number was believed to be much higher. The researchers also heard of babies who could not breastfeed and were surviving on mixtures of water and sugar. Amnesty spoke to two malnutrition health experts to understand the consequences of going for a prolonged period without adequate nutrition. Morna says children who survive for months eating animal feed can still suffer devastating long-term effects. ‘Malnutrition can affect children’s health, growth, and development, including those under five and older children. Its consequences can extend into the next generation. If girls experience stunted growth, for example, their ability to carry children may be compromised…’ Malnutrition can affect children’s health, growth, and development, including those under five and older children. Its consequences can extend into the next generation, she says. If girls experience stunted growth, for example, their ability to carry children may be compromised. Morna says the impact on children could be missed if an investigation relied only on adult survivors, satellite imagery, or video footage. Children’s accounts helped researchers understand what life under siege meant from day to day, including the difficulty of finding food and the particular risks faced by babies and young children. How researchers verified children’s accounts Morna says Amnesty approached interviews with children carefully, both to protect them from further harm and to test the reliability of the information gathered. Researchers often spoke to older children first. With younger children, they might not have access to the referral services and psychosocial support needed when recounting traumatic experiences. Morna says testimony from older children could be as credible as testimony from adults. As with any interviewee, researchers sought to verify what they heard by comparing accounts from different people and looking for corroborating evidence. That could include digital material relating to an incident, interviews with family members and, where relevant, health documentation. In a case involving the rape of a child, for example, researchers might also speak to the child’s mother about what she understood had happened. “We don’t rely on one person’s testimony,” Morna says, describing the process of cross-checking accounts. “We speak to multiple people and look for corroborating evidence.” ‘The effects of the conflict are not limited to immediate physical harm. None of the children interviewed had had access to education for several years…’ Years without education and the risk of further violence The effects of the conflict are not limited to immediate physical harm. Morna says none of the children Amnesty interviewed had had access to education for several years. Many were keen to continue their studies and had ambitions for the future, but their education had effectively stopped in El Fasher when the conflict broke out in 2023. Displacement had prevented them from returning to learning in any meaningful way. Morna warned that the loss of education could have long-term consequences for Sudan’s ability to rebuild its professional workforce and economy. She also highlighted the psychological effects of violence and displacement. Without support to address trauma, she says, there was a risk that cycles of violence could continue. When researchers asked older boys how they imagined their futures, some saw a choice between continuing their education where they had been displaced and returning to seek revenge on those who had destroyed their families. ‘Families were often dealing with several forms of trauma at once: relatives killed, fathers missing after detention and sisters who had been raped…’ Morna says families were often dealing with several forms of trauma at once: relatives killed, fathers missing after detention and sisters who had been raped. When families reached a displacement site or a relatively safer place, access to services was often limited, and their basic needs were not always met. That left few opportunities for children and adults to recover from what they had experienced. Many children had spent much of their lives in displacement around El Fasher. Some had been born in camps and barely knew their villages or where their families came from. They had grown up without the safety and stability needed to develop and contribute to society. Morna says Sudan would be dealing with the consequences for many years. Evidence of coordinated abuses The report also examined whether the violations documented in North Darfur were isolated acts by individual fighters or part of a wider campaign. Morna says Amnesty had identified two commanders in the report. Interviews with people who had been detained helped researchers understand the degree of control exercised by senior figures, she says, because detainees had repeated contact with particular commanders and a clearer understanding of the RSF network operating in the area. One commander named in the report was [Major General Gedo Hamdan Ahmed Mohamed (popularly known by his alias ‘Abu Shouk’]. Morna says researchers understood him to be responsible for much of the detention and oversight of detention in El Fasher. ‘The campaign is widespread, systematic, and coordinated… the pattern of violence is not made up of sporadic or one-off incidents. Research documented repeated cases of rape and sexual violence, killings, and detentions in particular towns, as well as the targeting of particular areas and ethnic groups…’ She describes the wider campaign as “widespread, systematic, and coordinated”, saying the pattern of violence was not made up of sporadic or one-off incidents. Researchers documented repeated cases of rape and sexual violence, killings, and detentions in particular towns, as well as the targeting of particular areas and ethnic groups. Morna says the consistency of the patterns across locations and individuals suggested that the abuses could not be explained simply as the actions of a few rogue fighters. “To me, that suggests a high degree of command responsibility,” she says. Senior leaders, she added, needed to be investigated both for what they had done and for what they had failed to do to control their forces. Amnesty calls for protection and accountability Morna says the international community should take more concrete action to protect civilians and make it more costly for those waging war to continue in this way. She called for greater scrutiny of the economic factors enabling the conflict, and says the United Arab Emirates had an important role in backing the RSF with resources, weapons, and other support. Cutting off some of those enablers, she argued, could change the course of the conflict. Amnesty also believes an independent, neutral protection force is needed on the ground, particularly in areas where violence is concentrated and civilians are repeatedly displaced in search of safety. Morna says the organisation was using the report to lobby for the international community to move towards authorising some form of protection presence. She describes this as a meaningful way to protect civilians. Accountability was another priority. Morna pointed to commanders such as Abu Lulu , who she says had filmed themselves committing atrocities and appeared to act with impunity. She argued that investigative mechanisms examining abuses in Sudan needed adequate resources and funding, and that international cases brought against alleged perpetrators should be supported. The aim, she says, should be to prevent the patterns of violence documented in North Darfur from being repeated elsewhere in Sudan, including in areas that have become new hotspots. ‘A window of opportunity’ Despite the scale of the abuses, Morna says she was hopeful that international attention on Sudan was changing. Since the launch of Amnesty’s report City Under Siege, Children Under Fire , the organisation had been engaged in advocacy. Morna says the response from media, international audiences, stakeholders, and states suggested that the conversation about Sudan was different from what it had been a year or two earlier. ‘Events in El Fasher are an important turning point in recognising the severity of the harm suffered by civilians…’ She describes the events in El Fasher as an important turning point in recognising the severity of the harm suffered by civilians. “There is an international community here that cares about what is happening in Sudan,” she says, adding that people were mobilising to try to act before the violence spread further. ‘The increased global attention creates a unique window and opportunity to press for meaningful and bold action…’ Morna says the increased global attention created a “unique window and opportunity” to press for meaningful and bold action. She had seen civil servants and humanitarian workers making efforts to engage, she says, and added that Sudan would remain a priority for Amnesty International. The long-term challenge, however, would extend well beyond the end of the fighting. Children who have endured sexual violence, hunger, displacement, and years without schooling will need sustained support if they are to recover and rebuild their lives. For Morna, documenting what has happened is only one part of the response. Protecting civilians, supporting investigations, and ensuring that senior figures are held accountable are also essential if the abuses describes in the report are not to be repeated. Transcript of interview: Radio Dabanga: Janine Morna, welcome to Radio Dabanga. To introduce you to our listeners, Janine is an Amnesty International human rights researcher specialising in children affected by armed conflict. Her current role at Amnesty is thematic researcher on children within Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme. She has researched conflicts in Niger, north-east Syria, Ukraine, Haiti, and Sudan. Last night, 1 October 2026, you spoke to an audience at De Balie, the venue in Amsterdam, about your report, which you partly initiated and co-authored, called City Under Siege, Children Under Fire . I want to focus on children, because what is happening to them is difficult to get your head around. You initiated this investigation, and much of your work at Amnesty focuses on children affected by armed conflict. What did you discover in North Darfur that made you conclude that children were not simply victims caught up in the violence, but were in some cases being deliberately targeted? Janine Morna: There are a couple of different violations specifically affecting children. I’m thinking in particular of the way boys are being targeted by the Rapid Support Forces to fight, herd livestock they use, and collect intelligence and information about potential opposing forces. We found this happened in two main ways. Groups allied with the Rapid Support Forces would often work with community leaders and others to mobilise young people—older boys, and sometimes younger boys as well—to fight alongside the RSF. In other cases, when the RSF attacked a particular village, young men and older boys would be abducted and forced or compelled to fight. We spoke to one RSF leader whose unit numbered about 90. He said that around 40 per cent of the unit was made up of young people. So, we’re looking at a very young population of men, younger boys and older boys helping to wage this violent campaign. Girls, in particular, are also being targeted for rape and sexual violence. When young women are rounded up, there is not necessarily any real consideration of their age or whether they are under 18. We documented a number of cases of rape and sexual violence. The youngest case, I think, involved a 13-year-old girl who was abducted and gang-raped repeatedly over several days. Time and again, we see that children are caught up in the killing, bombardment, and displacement, and suffer the same violations as adults. But they are also deliberately targeted for a range of other violations. Radio Dabanga: You interviewed 39 children as part of this investigation. What can children tell us about what happened in and around Darfur, and El Fasher specifically, that might otherwise be missed in an investigation based on adult survivors, satellite imagery, and videos? And how did you establish the credibility of their testimony while protecting them from further harm? Janine Morna: That’s a really important question. One reason we wanted to shed light on children, particularly in El Fasher, was the starvation that was happening at the time. One important distinction is that when an adult is unable to secure food, they may be able to survive in a way that children—and babies in particular—cannot. We tried to flesh this out in the report, because when a city is under siege, it can be difficult to understand what that means on the ground, day to day. We documented not only that children were not eating regularly, but also that four children had died because of the lack of available food. We believe the actual number was much higher. We looked at babies who were unable to breastfeed and were consequently surviving on mixtures of water and sugar. We spoke to two malnutrition health experts, I think, to understand the implications of going for a prolonged period without appropriate nutrition. Even if you survive several months eating animal feed, the long-term consequences can be devastating, particularly for children under five, but also for older children. Their health, growth and development can be affected, with consequences that can even pass from one generation to the next. For example, if young women and girls experience stunted growth, their ability to carry children can be compromised, affecting the next generation as well. It is really important for people to understand the disproportionate impact of the conflict. That can be difficult to capture if you speak only to adults or look at satellite imagery and other material. As for the credibility of the testimony, we often speak to older children first, for a number of reasons. We want to work ethically, and when children are younger, we may not have the appropriate referral services and psychosocial support to help them as they relive the trauma of describing their experiences. I find that the credibility of testimony from older children is almost the same as that of adults. We verify it in the same way: first, by triangulating information. If we document a particular attack, we don’t rely on one person’s testimony. We speak to multiple people and look for corroborating evidence. In our case, that can include digital evidence relating to the incident. In some cases, we speak to family members. For example, if a child has been raped, we might also interview her mother, who can provide her account of what she understands her child to have experienced, and review any health documentation. It is the same kind of triangulation that we would use for any interviewee. Radio Dabanga: That’s very clear. From our experience reporting for Radio Dabanga, and looking at the figures in your report, it seems this is only the tip of the iceberg: these are the cases you have managed to verify. The numbers are mind-blowing, almost difficult to take in. What have you observed among the children in Sudan you have spoken to? They have seen a great deal for their age, but are they precocious, or do you see a lack of development? Janine Morna: There are a couple of things I would note. None of the children we spoke to had had access to education for several years. You’re looking at really bright people with lots of aspirations. They want to engage and continue their education, which effectively stopped in El Fasher when the conflict broke out in 2023. They have not been able to continue it in any meaningful way while displaced. That has devastating intergenerational effects when it comes to developing a professional workforce that can return, help Sudan grow and rebuild its economy. Another major concern is that, unless the trauma and psychological pain caused by these experiences are addressed, cycles of violence will continue. When you speak to older boys about where they see their lives going, the choice can be: ‘Either I continue my education here, or I go back and get revenge on the people who have devastated and destroyed our families.’ That is why psychosocial support will be really important. People are experiencing unprecedented levels of trauma. Within a single family, there may be multiple deaths, a father missing because he was detained, and sisters who have been raped. Any one of those incidents is hard to process, but people are experiencing all these traumas compounded. When people reach a displacement site or somewhere relatively safer, they have very limited access to services. Some are not even in formal refugee camps, and their basic needs are not being met. The opportunities to heal, recover and process what has happened are already very limited. It is also important to note that El Fasher is surrounded by major camps for internally displaced people. Many children were born in displacement. They have barely known their villages or where they came from, because they have lived with conflict for almost their entire lives. These are people who have never experienced safety—the conditions people need in order to develop meaningfully and contribute to the economy. I think Sudan will be dealing with those long-term effects for many years to come. Radio Dabanga: What you say about people growing up without an environment of safety holds true for anyone in Sudan under 40, simply because there have been civil wars, especially in Darfur, and now there is conflict across the country. Amnesty says that some of the conduct documented in North Darfur amounts to crimes against humanity, and you mentioned that eight of the 11 crimes against humanity have been documented. What is the strongest evidence you have of a pattern of command responsibility, rather than simply individual acts of violence by fighters on the ground, as both sides say? Janine Morna: In the report, we name two commanders. We have been able to identify the level of control some senior commanders exercise partly through interviews with people who have been detained. Those individuals have repeated exposure to particular commanders and a much better understanding of the RSF network involved in the conflict in this context. One commander named in the report is quite senior and has been sanctioned by others: [Major General] Gedo Hamdan Ahmed Mohamed [popularly known by his alias/nom de guerre] ‘Abu Shouk’. We understand him to be responsible for much of the detention and oversight of detention in El Fasher, which we identify as one of the major violations. More broadly, if you look at the way this campaign of violence was waged, it was widespread, systematic, and coordinated. These were not sporadic events or one-off incidents; the patterns of violence were part and parcel of the way the Rapid Support Forces took over the area. These were not isolated acts, and I think that speaks to a degree of coordination within the RSF. The patterns are too consistent across locations and individuals to be explained as one-off acts by ‘bad actors’ or ‘bad apples’. There are multiple instances of rape and sexual violence in particular towns, multiple killings, and multiple detentions. Particular areas and ethnic groups are targeted. You can’t help but conclude that this comes from somewhere at the top, and that at a minimum these practices are accepted in the way the campaign of violence is being waged. To me, that suggests a high degree of command responsibility. Senior leaders need to be investigated for what they did, and what they failed to do, to control their forces. Radio Dabanga: Amnesty says some of the conduct documented in North Darfur relates to genocide, as you said. Having documented what happened to civilians, particularly children in El Fasher, what do you believe the international community needs to do differently now to prevent these patterns of violence from being repeated elsewhere in Sudan? We mentioned, for instance, El Obeid, which is now the latest hotspot, and the violence moves. So, what does the international community need to do tangibly, rather than just talk from the podium of the Security Council? What can it do concretely to end this war? Janine Morna: Well, certainly, from Amnesty International’s perspective, there are a number of actions it should be taking. First, you need to make the cost of waging war in this manner much higher. I think that includes the international community being much more engaged and outspoken about the economic enablers of the conflict. The United Arab Emirates has a really important role in backing the Rapid Support Forces with resources, weapons, and other support. Cutting off some of those economic enablers could really change the tide of the conflict. I think that’s really important. There must also be much bolder action in terms of what is happening on the ground. We certainly believe that a protection presence is necessary to secure the safety of civilians, particularly in those hotspot areas. We saw time and again people being continually displaced, looking for a safe place to be and not being able to find one. To secure safe places, we need an independent, neutral protection force on the ground. With this report, we are trying to lobby and advocate for the international community to move towards authorising some kind of protection presence. We believe it is the only really meaningful way to protect civilians. Then there is the need to pursue accountability. In El Fasher, you have commanders such as Abu Lulu filming themselves committing some of the worst atrocities on camera and acting with impunity. That gives you a sense of how much people perceive the international community cares about what is happening in Sudan. Pursuing accountability is so important. We need to make sure the investigative mechanisms established to investigate what is happening in Sudan are well resourced and well-funded, and have the opportunity to document these violations meaningfully. International cases brought against some of these perpetrators must also be supported. Radio Dabanga: That’s very clear. Thank you very much. To conclude, what message do you want to send to the listeners of Radio Dabanga? The bulk of our listeners are in Sudan. Our shortwave broadcasts can also be received in Chad, in the displacement camps and in all the places where there is no internet or telephone communication. Very often, we are the only source of information for people. Do you have a message of hope to send out? Janine Morna: Yes. The one thing I would say is that we have been doing a lot of advocacy since the launch of this report, and I am hopeful that the tide in Sudan is changing. If we look at the response from the media and international audiences that Amnesty International engages with, and even at stakeholders and states, the conversation about Sudan now is quite different from what might have happened a year or two ago. El Fasher really feels like an important turning point, a real recognition of the severity of the harm people are suffering. I want to say that there is an international community that cares about what is happening in Sudan and is mobilised to try to do something before the violence continues to spread. I think there is a unique window of opportunity to capitalise on increasing global attention on what is happening in Sudan and to motivate meaningful, bold action. I have seen many committed civil servants and humanitarian actors really trying to engage on this. Sudan will continue to be a priority country for Amnesty International. We want to see meaningful action by states, and we are mobilising our resources and remain committed to trying to make that happen. Radio Dabanga: Thank you very much, Janine, for talking to Radio Dabanga. We wish you every success with your research. And keep the facts and figures flowing, because they are really important to us as well, as we report the news on the ground. We hope to speak to you again soon. Janine Morna: Thank you. Thank you for having me. Share article The post Amnesty researcher: ‘Sudan’s children face recruitment, sexual violence, and lasting trauma’ appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

items.title: Haaland injury worry as Norway lose in Portugal
items.description: Erling Haaland sparked injury concerns as he limped off in Norway’s 2-1 Nations League defeat by Portugal. The Manchester City striker beckoned to the bench to be substituted in the 67th minute of the Group A4 tie. With seven goals so far this season, the club will await further news as they prepare for a trip to Liverpool on Sunday in the Premier League. It will be their first game since they were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League’s financial regulations. City have lodged an appeal. Haaland and Norway suffered a third successive Nations League defeat on Sunday as Goncalo Ramos scored a late winner for Portugal, who booked their place in the last eight. The hosts had to come from behind after the visitors took a 36th-minute lead. Brentford defender Kristoffer Ajer controlled Martin Odegaard’s cross on his chest before hitting a sweet half-volley into the top corner from the edge of the box. But two minutes later Joao Cancelo smashed home a stunning shot on the bounce from a similar distance from Nuno Mendes’ long throw-in. Haaland went close for Norway, dragging an effort wide, before he was replaced by Jorgen Strand Larsen. But it was Ramos who sealed a fourth successive win in the competition, stabbing in from close range from Joao Felix’s lay-off with 11 minutes left. Portugal ended with 10 men after winger Francisco Conceicao was sent off in the 87th minute for two quickfire bookings for dissent. It was their third game in a row without Cristiano Ronaldo in the team, after the country’s record scorer left the camp last week after being dropped. Boss Jorge Jesus plans to discuss the matter with the 41-year-old forward, but said on Sunday: “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team.” With two games left in the group stage, defending Nations League champions Portugal are now six points clear of second-placed Denmark, who beat Wales 1-0 , while Norway are bottom of the group.

items.title: Doune : Des bourses et fournitures scolaires pour les orphelins des agents disparus
items.description: Au-delà de la mobilisation des recettes et de la lutte contre la fraude, la Douane burkinabè soutient les familles de ses agents disparus. À l'initiative de la « Cellule Solidarité » de l’AIDF, et avec l'appui du Directeur général, le Dr Yves Kafando, des fournitures scolaires et des bourses d'études ont été remises à leurs orphelins, ce 3 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou. ​Ils sont une trentaine d'enfants à bénéficier du soutien des collègues de leurs parents décédés. Le don est composé de sacs, de fournitures scolaires, de deux cartons de savon et d'une enveloppe financière pour chaque enfant. ​Pour le Directeur général des douanes, le Dr Yves Kafando, même s'il est nécessaire de réaliser de bons rendements, il est tout aussi indispensable d'y associer le volet social. Selon lui, l'action du jour est en parfaite harmonie avec la vision du Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, qui ne cesse d'insister sur la prise en charge des veuves et orphelins. Une vision qui s'est d'ailleurs matérialisée par la création de l’Agence de soutien aux veuves, orphelins et victimes de guerre (ASVOVIG). ​S'adressant aux enfants, il a déclaré : « Nous sommes vos papas. Nous serons toujours là ». ​Le Dr Yves Kafando a par ailleurs traduit toute son admiration aux mères de ces enfants qui, malgré l'absence de leurs époux, se battent au quotidien : « Je fais une mention spéciale aux mères ici présentes qui se battent au quotidien pour que ces enfants puissent un jour se faire une place au soleil. (…) Il ne faut pas baisser les bras. Celui-là même qui vous parle est un orphelin de père et de mère. Cela ne m'a pas empêché d'être ce que je suis aujourd'hui » , a-t-il témoigné. ​Réunies au sein de l’Association des veuves et orphelins de la famille douanière (AVOFD), les mères des bénéficiaires n'ont pas caché leur joie. Pour elles, c'est une véritable épine retirée du pied. ​« Grâce à ce don, nos enfants iront tranquillement à l’école, sans inquiétude. Nous réitérons nos remerciements et notre profonde gratitude à l’endroit des donateurs, tout en souhaitant que cette activité soit pérennisée », a confié Alimata Maré/Ouédraogo, présidente de l'association. ​Pour cette première édition de remise de kits scolaires, les orphelins bénéficiaires sont des élèves du primaire ou admis en classe de 6ᵉ, dont les parents sont décédés dans l'exercice de leurs fonctions ou non. ​Pour le Président de la délégation nationale de l’AIDF, le Colonel des douanes David Goumroimama Onadja, ce don est loin d'être une charité : il le perçoit plutôt comme un devoir de mémoire. L'association ambitionne d'ailleurs d'étendre ce soutien aux orphelins des autres classes, y compris du supérieur. Tout dépendra des ressources mobilisées, d'autant plus que les contributions sont volontaires. ​De son côté, le Directeur général des douanes, très attaché à la vision du chef de l'État, a demandé la pérennisation de cette activité et a émis le souhait qu'elle fasse tâche d'huile dans d'autres administrations. ​Il est à noter que l’Association internationale des douaniers francophones (AIDF) est un réseau qui rassemble des agents de douane issus de pays ayant la langue française en partage. Bien qu'anglophone, le Nigeria est le dernier pays à y avoir adhéré. L’article Doune : Des bourses et fournitures scolaires pour les orphelins des agents disparus est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Portugal boss says door open for Ronaldo return
items.description: Cristiano Ronaldo can still return to Portugal if he chooses, says boss Jorge Jesus. The 41-year-old captain left their Nations League camp after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark. Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances – both world records. After leaving the camp, he wrote on social media: “In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated.” Jesus, for his part, had always said he planned to discuss the issue after the last of his side’s four Nations League games against Norway on Sunday. A 2-1 victory sealed a place in the last eight for the competition’s defending champions. Jesus – who also managed Ronaldo at Al-Nassr – said: “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team. “We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who’s going to decide. “Cristiano should end his time in the national team the way he wants, he’s the one who will decide how he wants it. “In my first call-up, I said, ‘I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying the same thing.” Portugal host Denmark in their next Group A4 tie on 14 November, before visiting Wales three days later. Ronaldo started the 1-0 opening-game win over Wales, but he was named as a substitute in Norway and told he may or may not come on. He was apparently angered at being made to warm up during the second half – and then not brought on. It was the first time the ex-Manchester United and Real Madrid forward had been an unused substitute for his country in a competitive game since 2008. When Jesus announced in a news conference Ronaldo would not start against Denmark either, the veteran left the camp. AC Milan striker Goncalo Ramos has scored in all three starts with Ronaldo out of the team. After Sunday’s success against Norway which put them six points clear of second-placed Denmark in the table, goalscorer Joao Cancelo told RTP: “Cristiano is our captain, the best player Portugal has ever had. “Things will certainly end in the best way [with him] but the important thing is the four victories.” Team-mate Nuno Mendes added: “Any player who comes to the national team is welcome, obviously. If Cris returns, we’ll be here to receive him with open arms.” Ronaldo, one of football’s all-time greats with five Ballon d’Or awards, has helped Portugal win Euro 2016 and two Nations Leagues.

items.title: Bellamy bemoans new schedule after Denmark loss
items.description: Craig Bellamy suggested the new four-match international window had counted against Wales after Sunday’s Nations League defeat against Denmark. His side failed to build on Thursday’s win over Norway, as they were deservedly beaten by a second-half Rasmus Hojlund penalty. It was the third loss in four games played within 10 days as part of the newly extended international break. Head coach Bellamy said his injury-hit squad paid the price for the heavy workload he feels benefits the bigger nations and “puts a real stress” on countries like Wales. “Physically, I completely agree with the ones who don’t like [the new window]. It makes no sense,” he added. “Four games at this type of level… for the other nations, we know who they are because I was in the room when they all voted for it. “I was one of the ones who wasn’t [voting for it], because we know it’s a complete disadvantage to us.” Traditionally, international sides have played six games across three windows – all of which have featured two fixtures – in September, October and November. But for the first time this year, the September and October breaks were merged. Wales’ hopes of coping with the new schedule were not helped by a string of injuries, with stars such as Karl Darlow, Joe Rodon, Dylan Lawlor and Harry Wilson missing the entire camp and David Brooks dropping out of the squad after defeat by Portugal in the opening game. Bellamy said Dan James was not fit enough to play against Denmark after he was left on the bench at the Cardiff City Stadium, and acknowledged Ben Davies probably should have been rested after he was withdrawn late on. “If we have a few injuries, which we had more than one or two, they miss four games,” said Bellamy. “We can deal with two, do you understand? And then the squad will get really tested. The intensity of the squad, the athleticism, really I think [the four-game break] is designed for the elites. “[They can] say, we can go, we can go, we can turn over these games really, really quickly and we can change, we can change [the team] like for like because we have the numbers. So, it puts a real stress on a lot of us.” Wales have three points from their first four games in this Nations League campaign Ward did ‘incredibly’ to keep it level before penalty Wales rarely looked like scoring against Denmark, who came close to breaking the deadlock on a couple of occasions before Hjolund’s 75th-minute winner. “On Thursday [against Norway] we were on the front foot so we’re able to shorten distance,” Bellamy added. “Today, we just couldn’t work it well enough, couldn’t get the energy up enough to be able to have a bigger say in the game.” Danny Ward made fine saves from Hojlund and Gustav Isaksen to keep Wales level but it was the goalkeeper’s error, and foul, which led to the penalty. Bellamy, though, suggested the game had not swung on Ward’s mistake, adding: “Obviously it’s the decisive moment, but he made two incredible saves before that. “I thought Denmark with the physicality were able to just crank it a little bit. You see their runs are really menacing, so I felt they were knocking on the door. He did incredibly well to keep it 0-0 to that time.” Despite defeat, Wales climbed to third in Nations League Group A4 courtesy of their head-to-head record against Norway after the Norwegians were beaten 2-1 in Portugal. Wales play Norway in Oslo next month before completing the campaign with a home game against Portugal three days later.

items.title: California heat wave breaks records, raises wildfire concerns
items.description: A prolonged heat wave continued across California over the weekend, breaking daily high-temperature records at multiple locations, while hot and dry conditions and wildfire smoke added to health and fire risks across parts of the state, according to the US National Weather Service (NWS) and state authorities. A preliminary report from the NWS San Diego office said eight daily high-temperature records were broken and one was tied on October 3 across Orange, San Diego and Riverside counties. Santa Ana in Orange County reached 41.7 degrees Celsius, about 2.8 degrees above the previous record for October 3 set in 2014, while Vista in San Diego County reached 42.2 degrees, according to the report. San Diego International Airport reached 40.6 degrees, breaking a daily record that had stood since 1987. The temperature was about 16.1 degrees above normal for the date, according to an NWS climate report. Farther north, Napa Airport reached 35.6 degrees, breaking its previous October 3 record of 34.4 degrees, according to the NWS San Francisco Bay Area office. In northern Nevada, Winnemucca Airport reached 32.2 degrees, breaking its previous daily record set in 2024, according to the NWS Elko office. The NWS Los Angeles/Oxnard office described the episode as a major and long-lasting heat wave and said unusually high temperatures were expected to persist through the coming week. More than 34 million Californians were under heat warnings or advisories. Extreme heat warnings remained in effect through Thursday evening in parts of Southern California, including San Diego and the coasts and valleys of Los Angeles and Ventura counties and parts of Santa Barbara County. The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) website listed several active incidents Sunday, including the Bouquet Fire in Los Angeles County, which had burned 1,048 acres and was 40% contained, and the Dome Fire in Mariposa County, which had burned 6,826 acres and was 40% contained. Across California, CAL FIRE reported 5,701 wildfires and 328,950 acres burned in 2026, with three fatalities and 157 structures destroyed. The figures are preliminary and subject to frequent updates. Smoke from active wildfires adds another health concern. Fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, can penetrate deep into the lungs and is particularly harmful to children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions, according to California health authorities. AirNow forecasts showed air quality reaching levels considered unhealthy for sensitive groups in several California communities on Sunday, with ozone identified as the main pollutant in a number of areas. Health officials advise residents to limit strenuous outdoor activity during periods of extreme heat or poor air quality, keep windows and doors closed when smoke is present, use air conditioning on recirculate and seek a cooler, cleaner-air location when necessary.

items.title: États-Unis : Christa Pike survit à une exécution par deux injections létales et reste dans un état critique
items.description: La condamnée qui a survécu à deux injections létales dans le Tennessee, Christa Pike, se trouvait toujours dans un état critique et sous assistance respiratoire, son pronostic vital étant encore inconnu, a affirmé dimanche sur CNN un de ses avocats, Stephen Ferrell. L'exécution ratée mercredi soir de Christa Pike, qui devait être la première femme mise à mort depuis plus de 200 ans au Tennessee (sud), a relancé les interrogations sur l'application de la peine capitale aux États-Unis. « Elle est toujours hospitalisée, sous assistance respiratoire et dans un état critique. Nous ne connaissons pas encore vraiment son pronostic vital et nous pourrions ne pas le connaître pendant plusieurs jours », a déclaré l'avocat. Stephen Ferrell a précisé ne pas avoir pu rendre visite à sa cliente, âgée de 50 ans, à l'hôpital où les médecins tentent toujours de retirer de son organisme les deux doses de pentobarbital, un puissant barbiturique, qui lui ont été administrées. Me Ferrell a de nouveau appelé le gouverneur du Tennessee, Bill Lee, à commuer sa peine. « À tout le moins, le gouverneur devrait commuer la peine de Mme Pike en prison à vie », a-t-il dit, estimant qu'elle a subi du fait de cette exécution ratée « une grave torture mentale et physique ». Le gouverneur, qui a ordonné jeudi la suspension des exécutions dans l'État et une enquête indépendante sur l'échec de celle de Christa Pike, a annoncé samedi avoir accepté la démission du chef de l'administration pénitentiaire du Tennessee (TDOC). L'administration pénitentiaire a affirmé avoir suivi à la lettre le protocole adopté depuis la reprise des exécutions dans l'État en mai 2025, après un moratoire de trois ans. Le gouverneur avait décrété ce moratoire à l'époque en raison de défaillances dans la vérification de la solution mortelle administrée à un condamné. L'observatoire spécialisé Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), a dénoncé jeudi « une exécution ratée sans comparaison à l'époque moderne », soulignant que Christa Pike est « la première personne à survivre à l'injection de doses létales de produits utilisés pour les exécutions ». Christa Pike a été condamnée à la peine capitale pour le meurtre en 1995 de Colleen Slemmer, 19 ans, alors qu'elle-même avait 18 ans. Ses deux complices, également adolescents, ont échappé à la peine de mort. items.title: La fin de «L’Aventure ambiguë» pour un «Gardien du Temple»
items.description: Ecrivain malgré lui, il fut tout de même, l’auteur de l’un des plus grands classiques de la littérature africains. Mort ce samedi 3 octobre 2026 à 98 ans, Cheikh Hamidou Kane dont le savoir immense a servi d’étoile polaire à nombre de combattants et de politiciens pour la souveraineté de l’Afrique, peut se targuer, malgré son humilité et sa volonté légendaires d’avoir partager son vécu et son expérience. Il ne s’est pas contenté de «lier le bois au bois», croulant sous le poids de diplômes obtenus à l’école et sur la terre du colonisateur, lui qui a été éduqué dans la pure et dure tradition islamique. A l’école coloniale où il s’est retrouvé pour apprendre «l’art de gagner la guerre sans avoir raison», Cheikh Hamidou Kane n’en n’était pas moins, comme ses contemporains, miné par l’angoisse existentielle de l’époque: ce qu’ils apprendront chez les blancs sera-t-il au prorata de ce qu’ils oublieront de la culture de leurs ancêtres? Et c’est l’essence de ce combat qui nourrissait la confrontation entre les anciens et les modernes. Ainsi se résumait le tournant décisif de la vie spirituelle non moins dichotomique, voire tumultueuse de Samba Diallo, le personnage principal, qui n’était que le personnage en fiction de Cheikh Hamidou Kane. Et ce n’est pas La Grande Royale, cette dame à la faute personnalité qui savait en imposer aux grands maîtres coraniques et aux chefs de la tradition, qui dira le contraire! Ce choix de savoir se servir des armes de l’ennemi pour le vaincre, aura été bien bénéfique pour Cheikh Hamidou Kane qui s’est forgé un bagage politique conséquent dans sa vie estudiantine pour servir de tremplin à l’indépendance et la souveraineté africaine, aux côtés de figures politiques comme Abdoulaye Wade, Joseph Ki-Zerbo, Léopold Sédar Senghor et Mamadou Dia. Notamment au sein de la Fédération des étudiant de l’Afrique, ils oeuvrèrent à enfoncer en terre, les premiers piliers intellectuels de la souveraineté du continent noir trop longtemps marqué au fer de la colonisation. A l’instar de Samba Diallo, ces intellectuels africains, pour exister et faire exister l’Afrique et ses cultures, ont donc décidé de penser, d’écrire et de réfléchir, par les armes du colonisateur. Et l’émotion n’était plus que nègre! Nonobstant le succès fulgurant et la profondeur philosophique de son premier roman, «L’Aventure ambiguë», publié en 1961, il a fallu attendre 1996 pour que Cheikh Hamidou Kane publie «Les Gardiens du Temple», demeurant ainsi dans sa profonde logique de mettre en confrontation, la tradition, les traditions que la colonisation n’avait de cesse d’effacer, et la modernité, joliment appelée progrès. Avec la disparition de Cheikh Kamidou Kane, comme le dit si bien la pensée africaine, c’est un baobab qui est tombé, c’est une bibliothèque qui a brûlé. Mais L’Aventure ambiguë est plus que jamais vivante sous l’œil vigilant des «Gardiens du Temple»! Par Wakat Séra L’article La fin de «L’Aventure ambiguë» pour un «Gardien du Temple» est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Présidentielle au Brésil : Flavio Bolsonaro surprend et affrontera Lula au second tour
items.description: Le sénateur conservateur Flavio Bolsonaro a créé la surprise dimanche au premier tour de la présidentielle au Brésil en devançant le président sortant de gauche Lula, qu'il affrontera au second tour le 25 octobre. Après dépouillement de près de 99 % des urnes, le fils de l'ex-chef de l'Etat d'extrême droite Jair Bolsonaro, âgé de 45 ans, obtient plus de 47 % des suffrages, contre près de 45% pour le vétéran de gauche Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80 ans. Le président des Etats-Unis, Donald Trump, avait dit suivre « de très près » l'élection brésilienne, après avoir vu des alliés parvenir au pouvoir en Argentine, en Colombie ou au Pérou. Les sondages prévoyaient un léger avantage pour Lula jusqu'à la veille du vote. Comme en 2018, les enquêtes d'opinion ont sous-estimé la force de la droite. Le scrutin avait alors mis aux prises Lula et Jair Bolsonaro. À bientôt 81 ans, Lula, qui brigue un quatrième et dernier mandat non consécutif, a durant la campagne appelé son homologue américain à ne pas « se mêler » des élections brésiliennes. Pour un coup d'essai, cela a presque été un coup de maître pour Flavio Bolsonaro. Il avait été désigné candidat par son père quand ce dernier a été condamné à 27 ans de prison pour une tentative de coup d'État contre Lula en 2022. Parmi les quelque 160 millions d'électeurs, beaucoup ont exprimé leur lassitude face à un casting si familier, et dit choisir le candidat qui leur déplaît le moins. « J'ai toujours voté pour Lula mais, une fois arrivée au bureau de vote, j'ai changé d'avis pour Bolsonaro. Juste pour essayer et voir ce que ça va donner », a déclaré à l'AFP Oscarina de Oliveira, 62 ans, auxiliaire de vie à Rio de Janeiro. « Le peuple devra choisir entre le renforcement du régime démocratique et la barbarie », a lancé le président sortant après avoir voté dans l'État de Sao Paulo (sud-est). À la sortie de son bureau de vote à Rio, le fils Bolsonaro a promis de « libérer le peuple brésilien ». « Le Brésil a besoin de changement, le Brésil ne supporte plus tant de souffrance, tant d'impôts élevés, tant de femmes tuées, tant de persécution politique », a-t-il affirmé. Inquiétudes et déceptions Les deux favoris avaient dit croire à une victoire dès dimanche, même si les sondages les montraient ces derniers jours encore assez loin des 50 %. Donald Trump n'a pas apporté son soutien à Flavio Bolsonaro, mais son influence a pesé sur la campagne. Il a dégainé droits de douane et sanctions contre le Brésil depuis le procès de 2025 contre son allié Jair Bolsonaro. « Je suis très inquiète de la direction que prend le pays, parce que je veux être indépendante, je ne veux être la colonie de personne », explique Maria de Nazaré Azevedo, fonctionnaire de 57 ans vivant à Rio. Elle a voté à gauche. « Nous votons pour Flavio Bolsonaro pour ne pas voter pour le PT. Ce parti a déjà passé vingt ans au gouvernement et n'a rien fait, vraiment rien », dit à Brasilia Raphael Machado, avocat de 45 ans, en référence au Parti des travailleurs de Lula. Revenu au pouvoir en 2023, le chef de l'État est reconnu pour ses programmes sociaux, qui ont sorti des millions de personnes de la pauvreté dans les années 2000. Mais les électeurs se plaignent du coût de la vie et de la criminalité galopante. Son adversaire a promis la manière forte contre le crime et l'austérité budgétaire. Défendre la nature Le fils Bolsonaro n'a pas perdu pied, après la révélation qu'il était visé par une enquête pour corruption et blanchiment d'argent sur le financement d'un film à la gloire de son géniteur. La droite ne manque pas de rappeler que Lula a passé en 2018-2019 plus de 18 mois en prison pour corruption, avant de voir sa condamnation annulée pour motifs de procédure. Dans son bilan, le vétéran de gauche affiche une baisse drastique de la déforestation en Amazonie, qui avait bondi sous la présidence Bolsonaro. Mais la question a brillé par son absence durant une campagne davantage semée de polémiques que de projets. « Nous, peuples autochtones, souffrons beaucoup des impacts environnementaux. Alors il est important de choisir un candidat qui défend notre territoire, qui défend la nature », a estimé Tainara da Costa Cruz, 22 ans. Membre de l'ethnie Kambeba, elle vit sur la rive du Rio Negro, près de la métropole amazonienne de Manaus, et a voté pour Lula.
